messages.subject: plumbing features through the interfaces
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

My apologies if this has already been discussed, but I was wondering how you guys handle features which touch simultaneously the different layers. So for example, let's say I write a neat new function in stan-math. This will affect stan and potentially cmdstan.

- Should I create now an issue in *all* repositories?
- And how can I make the changes in math available to code in stan when I am developing?

Is this somewhere on the wiki?

Thanks!

Sebastian

>
> - Should I create now an issue in *all* repositories?

I'd start with an issue in the language repo (if this is for something that ends up getting exposed in the interfaces) and get enough buy-in that you think it's going to make it through the process, then open an issue on stan-dev/math (if there's math to implement) once you know how it's going to be implemented).  The language seems to be the gatekeeper for the interfaces.  It makes sense since the interfaces mostly expose the language rather than providing another layer and once people start using a language feature we're sort of stuck with maintenance/deprecation management.

Krzysztof

Daniel --- can you dump this in the wiki somewhere with clarification?
I realized I don't know how to synch breaking updates.

I don't think so.  There are two cases.  Adding a new function to Stan
is easy.  It can go in math, then in Stan, then there's nothing to
change downstream.

Changing a behavior in math that then breaks stan is a different problem.
That usually doesn't happen.  But if it does, then we need pull requests
for both math and stan (and sometimes all the other interfaces),
because the math tests test integration with stan and above.

There's a make target in all the repos with sub-repos, as in make math-update
from Stan that brings you to current math w.r.t. branch of stan you are on, or
the current stan w.r.t. branch of cmdstan you are on (no idea how RStan, PyStan,
etc. do this).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
See below.

Daniel --- could you also drop the diagram below in the wiki page?

> On Apr 1, 2016, at 11:04 AM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> On Friday, April 1, 2016 at 7:12:33 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
>> Hi!
>>
>> My apologies if this has already been discussed, but I was wondering how you guys handle features which touch simultaneously the different layers. So for example, let's say I write a neat new function in stan-math. This will affect stan and potentially cmdstan.
>>
>> - Should I create now an issue in *all* repositories?
>
> I'd start with an issue in the language repo (if this is for something that ends up getting exposed in the interfaces) and get enough buy-in that you think it's going to make it through the process, then open an issue on stan-dev/math (if there's math to implement) once you know how it's going to be implemented).

> The language seems to be the gatekeeper for the interfaces.

The language isn't usually the issue, though we are picky about it
because we don't want to break people's models, so we want to be careful
with naming, etc.   The language itself only interfaces through the model
class that gets generated in C++.

It's just that everything has to be consistent.

> It makes sense since the interfaces mostly expose the language rather than providing another layer and once people start using a language feature we're sort of stuck with maintenance/deprecation management.

The bigger picture is this, and you see the stan-dev/stan repo really
spans three logical layers:

                      stan
          ----------------------------------
  math <- language <- algorithms <- services <- pystan
                                             <- rstan   <- rstanarm
                                                        <- rethinking
                                             <- cmdstan <- statastan
                                                        <- matlabstan
                                                        <- stan.jl

What we are trying to do with the services refactor is make a clean
services layer between the core interfaces (pystan, rstan, cmdstan) so that
these don't have to know anything below the services layer.   Ideally,
there wouldn't be any calls from pystan, rstan, or cmdstan other than
ones to the stan::services namespace.  services, on the other hand, is
almost certainly going to need to know about things below the algorithms
level in language and math.

- Bob

>
> p(d|theta) as a function of theta is the likelihood L(d|theta) which
> is not a probability distribution. Sometimes it's proportional to a
> probability distribution (posterior) and sometimes prior is required
> to make it possible to normalise the posterior.

This is not entirely true — any conditional probability distribution,
p[ E | theta ], is a probability distribution for any theta in the
second argument and a measurable function for any E in the
first argument.  They are mathematically the same object.

The distinction I think you are trying to get at is more subtle,
and involves not just the likelihood but also the marginal
likelihood.  When we update from the prior to the posterior
measure theoretically we need a function,

P^{post} [E_{Theta} | d ] = (dP^{post} / dP^{prior})(theta)  P^{prior} [ E_{Theta} ]
P^{post} [E_{Theta} | d ] \equiv f(theta) P^{prior} [ E_{Theta} ].

f is the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the posterior with respect
to the prior, but is also the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the
likelihood with respect to the marginal likelihood (this is basically
the measure theoretical version of Bayes’ Theorem).

So the ambiguity that can arise is between the likelihood
(a conditional probability distribution) and this updating
function (a Radon-Nikodym derivative).  But because you
need measure theory to make all of this make sense, and
it doesn’t really affect any practical use of Bayes, I don’t
think it’s all that helpful to discuss.

Cool!

The C++11 is the real killer for compatiblity, but that's
less of an issue with CmdStan than anything else.  Especially
if compiling the relevant translation unit is made optional.

I assume the C++11 is for the thread support.  Is postgres slow
enough that it needs a dedicated thread?  Can we still run four
processes for four chains in parallel?  If so, then we'll need
8 cores to run 4 chains if that postgres thread is really necessary.
If the postgres thread is underutilitized, it might make sense to
just remove the C++11 and threading dependency.  If it's all latency
but the throughput is OK (often the case with network I/O), then it
might make sense to buffer.

- Bob

Yeah, once I made the decision to go that route other things probably
snuck in but threading is the main thing.

It's the throughput.  All my (informal) timing was on a dual-core laptop
(four "cores") with a solid state disk and the database on the same machine.
I wanted to avoid diving into the postgres C library and the libpqxx C++ library
has this nice layer that will do transactions wrapped in another layer that checks
on connection failures and re-tries anything that fails.  There's probably
room for improvement but writing code that's both fast AND resilient to
network problems is going to be hard.

I tried some informal timings (100 iterations of 1,000 parameters and 100 iterations of
100,000 parameters) and it looks like the on-the-fly munging the writer does
along with the postgres writes takes about as much CPU time as running Stan
so it's a deal breaker (for me) if they need to share a thread but the current
design is that the writer piles work onto a queue and has a thread (or a few) that
pick up work and write it.  It'll make sense to do real timing tests once I have
this thing in the context of CmdStan and some real models.

Krzysztof

My thoughts about this have been influenced, e,g, by A. P. Dawid who has wrote the following

By A.P. Dawid
-------------------------------------------------------------------------

In a (doubtless ill-fated) attempt to explain more clearly the
essential distinction between a STATISTICAL MODEL and a LIKELIHOOD
FUNCTION --- one that until recently was widely understood but now
seems to engender great confusion --- I will try and make the point
as concrete as possible.

I am fishing.  Everybody agrees that fish will bite according to a
Poisson process (hence the name!) of some rate \lambda bites per
hour.  \lambda is unknown and we wish to make some inference about
\lambda from observing my performance.

Observer O1 plans to turn up after 3 hours and find out how many
fish, N, I have caught.

The STATISTICAL MODEL for N is the Poisson family Po(\lambda), with
discrete probability mass function:

(1)  p_1( n | \lambda) = \exp{- 3 \lambda} \lambda^n /n!
      (n = 0, 1, ...; \lambda >0 )

Observer O2 asks me to call her mobile as soon as I have caught 12
fishes. She will note the time T of this event.

The STATISTICAL MODEL for T is a Gamma family, Ga(12, \lambda),
with continuous probability density function:

(2)  p_2( t | \lambda) = (\lambda^{12}/ 11!) t^{11}  \exp{ -\lambda t}
      (t > 0; \lambda > 0)

Now it so happens that I catch my 12th fish after exactly 3 hours.
Thus O1 observes N=12, while O2 observes T=3.  Even though they
have ** utterly different ** STATISTICAL MODELS, involving even
different variables and different sample spaces, for this
particular outcome both O1 and O2 agree that the LIKELIHOOD
FUNCTION for \lambda (i.e. p_1( 12 | \lambda) for O1, p_2( 3 |
\lambda) for O2) is proportional to

(3)  L(\lambda) = \lambda^{12} \exp{ -3 \lambda}
      (\lambda > 0)

Indeed, I too Would obtain this, using as my STATISTICAL MODEL the
full Poisson process, and as my data the complete record of my
performance (i.e. exactly when each fish was caught) in the first 3
hours.

In no sense is (3) a PROBABILITY DISTRIBUTION for anything (or even
a probability for anything).

This example can be used to make various points about the
likelihood principle, optional stopping, sufficiency, etc. --- but
I will leave it there for now.

I surmise that one reason for the current confusion is the
(correct) statement that, in order to calculate a posterior
distribution we need both a prior distribution and a likelihood.
In fact it is only the ``observed'' likelihood function (e.g. (3)
in the story above) that is required.  But typically we will have
started from a fully specified STATISTICAL MODEL, using this to
derive the relevant observed LIKELIHOOD FUNCTION.  Because of this
link the distinction between the two has been elided.

Phil

-------------------------------------------------------------------------

University College London, Gower Street, London WC1E 6BT, United Kingdom.

E-mail:			da...@stats.ucl.ac.uk

messages.body_plain:
Phil is making the same mistake, conflating the likelihood
(a collection of probability distributions over data from a
frequentist perspective of a conditional probability distribution
from a Bayesian perspective) with the Radon-Nikodym
derivative that gets used in updating (what he calls the
“observed” likelihood).

The likelihood is a conditional probability distribution, so
if we plug in any data event then we get a function from
parameters to probabilities,

L[E_{D} | theta ] : theta \mapsto [0, 1].

But that’s not all that useful because we’ll mostly be
considering point events which have zero measure,
so this map degenerates to mapping everything to zero.

We could look at the corresponding conditional probability
density function l(d | theta), but then this depends on the
sample space.  It’s why you get different density functions
if you’re looking at counts or time in Phil’s example.

When we’re performing a Bayesian update we care
about neither of these.  We care only about the the

Radon-Nikodym derivative of the likelihood with respect

to the marginal likelihood,

f(d, theta) = dL_{conditional} / dL_{marginal} = l (d | theta} / l(d).

This is now a map from a point in data space and a parameter
to a real number, and we can plug in the observed data to
update our prior to our posterior,

P_{post} = f(d, theta) P_{prior}.

Now here’s the cool thing — f(d, theta) is invariant under
measurable maps.  You can see this from the density
representation — the Jacobians cancel in the ratio.  So
the actual learning is invariant to the sample space we
use to express the measurements, as it should be!  This
is why in Phil’s example the “observed” likelihood was
invariant.  But it’s really the observed likelihood/marginal
likelihood ratio that’s true invariant.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the additional explanation. I now accept that likelihood is a conditional probability distribution.

Aki

On Saturday, April 2, 2016 at 1:30:59 PM UTC+3, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Phil is making the same mistake, conflating the likelihood
> (a collection of probability distributions over data from a
> frequentist perspective of a conditional probability distribution
> from a Bayesian perspective) with the Radon-Nikodym
> derivative that gets used in updating (what he calls the
> “observed” likelihood).
>
> The likelihood is a conditional probability distribution, so
> if we plug in any data event then we get a function from
> parameters to probabilities,
>
> L[E_{D} | theta ] : theta \mapsto [0, 1].
>
> But that’s not all that useful because we’ll mostly be
> considering point events which have zero measure,
> so this map degenerates to mapping everything to zero.
>
> We could look at the corresponding conditional probability
> density function l(d | theta), but then this depends on the
> sample space.  It’s why you get different density functions
> if you’re looking at counts or time in Phil’s example.
>
> When we’re performing a Bayesian update we care
> about neither of these.  We care only about the the
> Radon-Nikodym derivative of the likelihood with respect
> to the marginal likelihood,
>
> f(d, theta) = dL_{conditional} / dL_{marginal} = l (d | theta} / l(d).
>
> This is now a map from a point in data space and a parameter
> to a real number, and we can plug in the observed data to
> update our prior to our posterior,
>
> P_{post} = f(d, theta) P_{prior}.
>
> Now here’s the cool thing — f(d, theta) is invariant under
> measurable maps.  You can see this from the density
> representation — the Jacobians cancel in the ratio.  So
> the actual learning is invariant to the sample space we
> use to express the measurements, as it should be!  This
> is why in Phil’s example the “observed” likelihood was
> invariant.  But it’s really the observed likelihood/marginal
> likelihood ratio that’s true invariant.
>
> On Apr 2, 2016, at 8:03 AM, Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:
>
> > My thoughts about this have been influenced, e,g, by A. P. Dawid who has wrote the following
> >
> > By A.P. Dawid
> > -------------------------------------------------------------------------
> >
> > In a (doubtless ill-fated) attempt to explain more clearly the
> > essential distinction between a STATISTICAL MODEL and a LIKELIHOOD
> > FUNCTION --- one that until recently was widely understood but now
> > seems to engender great confusion --- I will try and make the point
> > as concrete as possible.
> >
> > I am fishing.  Everybody agrees that fish will bite according to a
> > Poisson process (hence the name!) of some rate \lambda bites per
> > hour.  \lambda is unknown and we wish to make some inference about
> > \lambda from observing my performance.
> >
> > Observer O1 plans to turn up after 3 hours and find out how many
> > fish, N, I have caught.
> >
> > The STATISTICAL MODEL for N is the Poisson family Po(\lambda), with
> > discrete probability mass function:
> >
> > (1)  p_1( n | \lambda) = \exp{- 3 \lambda} \lambda^n /n!
> >      (n = 0, 1, ...; \lambda >0 )
> >
> > Observer O2 asks me to call her mobile as soon as I have caught 12
> > fishes. She will note the time T of this event.
> >
> > The STATISTICAL MODEL for T is a Gamma family, Ga(12, \lambda),
> > with continuous probability density function:
> >
> > (2)  p_2( t | \lambda) = (\lambda^{12}/ 11!) t^{11}  \exp{ -\lambda t}
> >      (t > 0; \lambda > 0)
> >
> > Now it so happens that I catch my 12th fish after exactly 3 hours.
> > Thus O1 observes N=12, while O2 observes T=3.  Even though they
> > have ** utterly different ** STATISTICAL MODELS, involving even
> > different variables and different sample spaces, for this
> > particular outcome both O1 and O2 agree that the LIKELIHOOD
> > FUNCTION for \lambda (i.e. p_1( 12 | \lambda) for O1, p_2( 3 |
> > \lambda) for O2) is proportional to
> >
> > (3)  L(\lambda) = \lambda^{12} \exp{ -3 \lambda}
> >      (\lambda > 0)
> >
> > Indeed, I too Would obtain this, using as my STATISTICAL MODEL the
> > full Poisson process, and as my data the complete record of my
> > performance (i.e. exactly when each fish was caught) in the first 3
> > hours.
> >
> > In no sense is (3) a PROBABILITY DISTRIBUTION for anything (or even
> > a probability for anything).
> >
> > This example can be used to make various points about the
> > likelihood principle, optional stopping, sufficiency, etc. --- but
> > I will leave it there for now.
> >
> > I surmise that one reason for the current confusion is the
> > (correct) statement that, in order to calculate a posterior
> > distribution we need both a prior distribution and a likelihood.
> > In fact it is only the ``observed'' likelihood function (e.g. (3)
> > in the story above) that is required.  But typically we will have
> > started from a fully specified STATISTICAL MODEL, using this to
> > derive the relevant observed LIKELIHOOD FUNCTION.  Because of this
> > link the distinction between the two has been elided.
> >
> > Phil
> >
> > -------------------------------------------------------------------------
> > A. P. Dawid, Professor of Statistics, Department of Statistical Science,
> > University College London, Gower Street, London WC1E 6BT, United Kingdom.
> > Tel:+44 (0)20 7679 1861				Fax: +44 (0)20 7383 4703
> > E-mail:			da...@stats.ucl.ac.uk
> > Personal web page:	http://tinyurl.com/2675a
> > Department web page:	http://www.ucl.ac.uk/Stats/
> > -------------------------------------------------------------------------
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > On Friday, April 1, 2016 at 9:26:03 PM UTC+3, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> >> p(d|theta) as a function of d is conditional probability distribution.
> >>
> >> p(d|theta) as a function of theta is the likelihood L(d|theta) which
> >> is not a probability distribution. Sometimes it's proportional to a
> >> probability distribution (posterior) and sometimes prior is required
> >> to make it possible to normalise the posterior.
> >>
> >> This is not entirely true — any conditional probability distribution,
> >> p[ E | theta ], is a probability distribution for any theta in the
> >> second argument and a measurable function for any E in the
> >> first argument.  They are mathematically the same object.
> >>
> >>
> >> The distinction I think you are trying to get at is more subtle,
> >> and involves not just the likelihood but also the marginal
> >> likelihood.  When we update from the prior to the posterior
> >> measure theoretically we need a function,
> >>
> >>
> >> P^{post} [E_{Theta} | d ] = (dP^{post} / dP^{prior})(theta)  P^{prior} [ E_{Theta} ]
> >> P^{post} [E_{Theta} | d ] \equiv f(theta) P^{prior} [ E_{Theta} ].
> >>
> >>
> >> f is the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the posterior with respect
> >> to the prior, but is also the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the
> >> likelihood with respect to the marginal likelihood (this is basically
> >> the measure theoretical version of Bayes’ Theorem).
> >>
> >>
> >> So the ambiguity that can arise is between the likelihood
> >> (a conditional probability distribution) and this updating
> >> function (a Radon-Nikodym derivative).  But because you
> >> need measure theory to make all of this make sense, and
> >> it doesn’t really affect any practical use of Bayes, I don’t
> >> think it’s all that helpful to discuss.
> >

I really like The Pragmatic Programmer by Hunt and Thomas.
And the original Extreme Programming book is also good (it
was the basis of Agile, which somehow missed the original
message and turned into another process).  Some people like
Steve McConnell's Code Complete, which is a bit more dry
than the other two, but still good.  And there may be more
things out there since I was in the market for a book like
this as I made the move from academia to industry.  For
code, I really like Martin Fowler's Refactoring book, but
it's all Java.  For all the C++ template stuff, there's
Vandevoorde and Josuttis's book, which is great, and also
Alexandrescu's Modern C++ Design.  These are all waiting
on C++ 11 updates, but they're way better than anything else
I've seen.  Effective C++ by Scott Myers is also good;  we're
not using C++11 yet, so all of the pre-C++11 versions would
be more relevant.  I need to start studying up on C++!

messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, April 2, 2016 at 3:57:30 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Yikes.  Is it a very easy Stan model with lots of parameters?

Once I have it in CmdStan it'll be simpler to see how the two parts work together. I think a model drawing N iterations of K N(0,1) variables per
iteration would be a good test.

> I'd think you'd want to wrap a buffered commit and make the
> whole thing transactional in order to report back, but wouldn't
> want to commit as you go.  Or is the whole reason you're doing this
> to allow saving intermediate state if something goes wrong?

I'd like to do this more or less as streaming because I want to see
the output as it's produced.  At the moment one iteration (however
many parameters) is one transaction.  It's actually really fast
for the main thread because the parameters are just copied
copied (as a std::vector<double> into a std::queue<std::vector<double>>
and the main thread moves on (to the next Stan iteration).  The worker threads then take iterations off the queue and now that I've gotten std::chrono figured out it looks like it takes ~1 second per 1,000 parameters CPU time per worker thread.  Since this is 1 insert per parameter it's about on par with what people seem to cite as the kind of performance you get form unoptimized inserts.  It is a little shocking how fast the .csv writer is in comparison (0.3ms for 1,000 parameters with similar instrumentation on the operator()(std::vector<double>))

I'm thinking of this in the context of a model with ~40k parameters that
takes maybe 8+ hours (?) to run.  With a single worker thread that
would be about 11 hours of time getting everything written into the DB
and no real increase to the Stan run-time---the workers just finish
processing/writing iterations after the sampler is done. With two worker
threads they stay ahead of the sampler.  On a multi-core desktop with 32GB RAM it's really fine.

I tend to work from a laptop and run Stan on a server/desktop I access from the command line. The second half of the workflow is that I can access Stan output in postgres directly from my laptop with R/dplyr (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dplyr/vignettes/databases.html) without worrying whether I need to move a 500MB csv file or try to read it over a network filesystem.

There's a moderate size cottage industry (and
slew of stack overflow Q&A) around optimizing writes to postgres
with a lot of good stuff I could use.  The code I wrote is clearly doing some things in the least efficient way possible.  Worst case I could be reducing the write time  quite a bit by writing each iteration as binary to the db and having a trigger that unpacks it on the db side.  Point is, there are lots of ways of optimizing this, but in the meantime it's not looking too bad.

Krzysztof

> - Bob
>
>
> > On Apr 1, 2016, at 4:18 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > On Friday, April 1, 2016 at 3:27:21 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >> Cool!
> >>

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the analysis.  That's really helpful.

I would have thought the right transaction granularity (for
both semantics and streaming speed) would be a row (iteration) rather
than a parameter.  Given that there's per-transaction disk overhead
plus handshake latency, this could make a big difference (that'll vary
by number of parameters).

I've never really worked directly with databases, so don't really
know what to expect from throughput.  Inverted indexes for text
search are pretty fast to write by comparison (without transactional
support).

The CSV writer is already slow compared to a binary writer;
.3ms per 1K params is 3M double values/second, which is
only 24MB/second of raw binary data, which is something like an order of
of magnitude under disk throughput.  It's usually the latency of writes
that's the killer, with solid states being way better than spinny disks,
which are in turn way better than most network storage options.

- Bob

>> I'd think you'd want to wrap a buffered commit and make the
>> whole thing transactional in order to report back, but wouldn't

>> to allow saving intermediate state if something goes wrong?

> the output as it's produced.  At the moment one iteration (however
> many parameters) is one transaction.  It's actually really fast
> for the main thread because the parameters are just copied
> copied (as a std::vector<double> into a std::queue<std::vector<double>>
> and the main thread moves on (to the next Stan iteration).  The worker threads then take iterations off the queue and now that I've gotten std::chrono figured out it looks like it takes ~1 second per 1,000 parameters CPU time per worker thread.  Since this is 1 insert per parameter it's about on par with what people seem to cite as the kind of performance you get form unoptimized inserts.  It is a little shocking how fast the .csv writer is in comparison (0.3ms for 1,000 parameters with similar instrumentation on the operator()(std::vector<double>))
>
> I'm thinking of this in the context of a model with ~40k parameters that
> takes maybe 8+ hours (?) to run.  With a single worker thread that
> would be about 11 hours of time getting everything written into the DB
> and no real increase to the Stan run-time---the workers just finish
> processing/writing iterations after the sampler is done. With two worker
> threads they stay ahead of the sampler.  On a multi-core desktop with 32GB RAM it's really fine.
>
> I tend to work from a laptop and run Stan on a server/desktop I access from the command line. The second half of the workflow is that I can access Stan output in postgres directly from my laptop with R/dplyr (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dplyr/vignettes/databases.html) without worrying whether I need to move a 500MB csv file or try to read it over a network filesystem.
>
> There's a moderate size cottage industry (and
> slew of stack overflow Q&A) around optimizing writes to postgres
> with a lot of good stuff I could use.  The code I wrote is clearly doing some things in the least efficient way possible.  Worst case I could be reducing the write time  quite a bit by writing each iteration as binary to the db and having a trigger that unpacks it on the db side.  Point is, there are lots of ways of optimizing this, but in the meantime it's not looking too bad.

messages.subject: Services and algorithm split
messages.body_plain:
Bob,

Thanks for putting together this diagram.

On Fri, Apr 1, 2016 at 12:58 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> The bigger picture is this, and you see the stan-dev/stan repo really
> spans three logical layers:
>
>                       stan
>           ----------------------------------
>   math <- language <- algorithms <- services <- pystan
>                                              <- rstan   <- rstanarm
>                                                         <- rethinking
>                                              <- cmdstan <- statastan
>                                                         <- matlabstan
>                                                         <- stan.jl
>
> What we are trying to do with the services refactor is make a clean
> services layer between the core interfaces (pystan, rstan, cmdstan) so that
> these don't have to know anything below the services layer.   Ideally,
> there wouldn't be any calls from pystan, rstan, or cmdstan other than
> ones to the stan::services namespace.  services, on the other hand, is
> almost certainly going to need to know about things below the algorithms
> level in language and math.
>

This clarified a lot of things. I think this is what we should do:
1. Split algorithms and services into their own repos. (Language too, but that's a given.)
2. Each "route" to calling an algorithm should live in the "algorithms" repo. That is, algorithms should expose a simple function for calling it directly. It'll be a C++ API, but not ones that the interfaces use directly.
3. In "services," we'll have a config object with validation and only a handful of calls that pystan, rstan, cmdstan call. The config object needs to be simple and safe, but I think the pseudocode Bob and I created (which is looking really close to Michael's config object if it were safe) will suffice.

Does that make sense?

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Probably better on the list rather than a comment on the running CVODES issue...

So here are the results for a hierarchical PK/PD model. To be specific, I simulated 50 patients of a 2-cmt model oral dosing situation for typical parameter values I use to see. Two doses (t=0 and t=24) are given and I compare against an analytic solution which I placed on the very left of the plots with abs_tol=1E-16 for machine precision. Now, I had to use the CVODES implementation as the CVODE+coupled integrator which is currently in develop did freeze Stan for 3 days while CVODES returned the results in a few hours, depending on the abs+rel tolerance set. I used a 1E-9, 1E-6 and a 1E-3 abs+rel tolerance. Have a look yourself, but I can't find any threshold of the ODE solver which seems to invalidate/bias results. I used 4 chains and per chain I did 500 warmups and 500 iterations. True values are

   theta_true <-  c(0.326634259978281, 0, 2.30258509299405, 1.6094379124341, 3.68887945411394)
  omega_true <-  c(0.3, 0.4)
  sigma_y_true <- 0.2

Any comments for improvements on the comparisons are very welcome.

Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Services and algorithm split
messages.body_plain:
On 04/04, Daniel Lee wrote:
> Bob,
>
> Thanks for putting together this diagram.
>
> On Fri, Apr 1, 2016 at 12:58 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> >
> > The bigger picture is this, and you see the stan-dev/stan repo really
> > spans three logical layers:
> >
> >                       stan
> >           ----------------------------------
> >   math <- language <- algorithms <- services <- pystan
> >                                              <- rstan   <- rstanarm
> >                                                         <- rethinking
> >                                              <- cmdstan <- statastan
> >                                                         <- matlabstan
> >                                                         <- stan.jl
> >
> > What we are trying to do with the services refactor is make a clean
> > services layer between the core interfaces (pystan, rstan, cmdstan) so that
> > these don't have to know anything below the services layer.   Ideally,
> > there wouldn't be any calls from pystan, rstan, or cmdstan other than
> > ones to the stan::services namespace.  services, on the other hand, is
> > almost certainly going to need to know about things below the algorithms
> > level in language and math.
> >
> >
> This clarified a lot of things. I think this is what we should do:
> 1. Split algorithms and services into their own repos. (Language too, but
> that's a given.)
> 2. Each "route" to calling an algorithm should live in the "algorithms"
> repo. That is, algorithms should expose a simple function for calling it
> directly. It'll be a C++ API, but not ones that the interfaces use directly.
> 3. In "services," we'll have a config object with validation and only a
> handful of calls that pystan, rstan, cmdstan call. The config object needs
> to be simple and safe, but I think the pseudocode Bob and I created (which
> is looking really close to Michael's config object if it were safe) will
> suffice.
>
> Does that make sense?

This sounds like an excellent idea. I think splitting up these parts
into repositories (and including something like this figure in the
READMEs) would help make Stan much more intelligible to interested
parties and potential contributors.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ODE Examples for Testing
messages.body_plain:
The warnings about y being negative are fine, but they should be seen only in warmup.
The infinity warnings are more pathological, but they could simply be an indication of
poor warmup.  The -4 CVODE error is failed convergence of the linear step in the solver,
which is fine, especially given the pathological states you’re seeing.  On my laptop I don’t
see such extreme pathologies, but I also ran with an initial step size of 0.001 and might
have and a better random seed.

sir_truth.stan is the true evolution of the SIR states in columns of time, y1, y2, y3, and y4.
The true vales are

beta =  1
gamma = 0.2

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ode tolerances / MCMC bias
messages.body_plain:
Regardless of the settings it looks like the MCMC estimators using CVODES vary by between
0.1 and 1%, which is not huge but still significant.  What is particularly troubling is that this is
larger than the standard error in each of the example, which means that the CVODES variation
is the dominate source of error.  This completely changes how we would have to report fits
that use ODE solvers.  Is there any intuition to why this variation is so strong and there is no
apparently convergence?

On Apr 4, 2016, at 6:57 PM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi!
>
> Probably better on the list rather than a comment on the running CVODES issue...
>
> So here are the results for a hierarchical PK/PD model. To be specific, I simulated 50 patients of a 2-cmt model oral dosing situation for typical parameter values I use to see. Two doses (t=0 and t=24) are given and I compare against an analytic solution which I placed on the very left of the plots with abs_tol=1E-16 for machine precision. Now, I had to use the CVODES implementation as the CVODE+coupled integrator which is currently in develop did freeze Stan for 3 days while CVODES returned the results in a few hours, depending on the abs+rel tolerance set. I used a 1E-9, 1E-6 and a 1E-3 abs+rel tolerance. Have a look yourself, but I can't find any threshold of the ODE solver which seems to invalidate/bias results. I used 4 chains and per chain I did 500 warmups and 500 iterations. True values are
>

> Sebastian

Hi,

I was trying to use the wiki page on contributing Stan functions (https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Contributing-New-Functions-to-Stan) to debug an issue yesterday, but some of the information on the page is out of date or not there. For instance,

1) When I look in src from Stan, there isn't a src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/ directory.

2) I can make test-headers, but when I try to make test-unit, I get the message that there's no rule to make it.

3) I didn't realize that for functions in src/test/test-models/good/function-signatures/math/functions/, you can make the models there by typing make src/test/test-models/good/function-signatures/math/functions/<function-name>.hpp-test. Also, on that note, where are the unit tests? The example given is for src/test/unit-agrad-rev/functions/log_test.cpp, but unit-grad-rev isn't a folder in src/test.

Could someone please look through and update the wiki page?

Thanks.

Best,
Rayleigh

Hi!

@Krysztof: Great to know that you also have a stake at ODEs.

>From the discussion earlier I figured the quickest thing to do is to repeat the plots I have done, but this time I split by chain which is now color coded. So each color corresponds to the same seed and the same chain id at different values of abs+rel tol passed to the ODE integrator (500 warmup/500 iterations). Note that the seed for the parameters is the same for all runs, only the chain_id varied while the stan_seed is also the same everywhere. Moreover, in the plots I am sending around what is declared in the Stan model as parameter is

theta, omega, sigma

The other quantities are derived from these. This time I also include the low precision runs from this morning. I think one can see a threshold which is 1E-2 where inferences seem to be consistently pulled into one direction. For the other abs/rel tolerances, from my view on it, I think it is hard to say anything. For me from 1E-6 (including) and onwards everything looks really ok. Although, one would probably have to run more chains and run an ANOVA against it to see if the abs/rel tolerance has an impact.

Cheers,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ode tolerances / MCMC bias
messages.body_plain:
I take it this is CVODES and perfect behavior would
be overlayed horizontal lines at the true answer.  So
the question is what's good enough?

What I'd like is some criterion by which we
can make decisions on which of these to keep:

   * Boost
   * CVODE
   * CVODES

Asked another way, what does Sebastian need to do to convince
everyone that CVODEs should go in?   At that point, is there
any reason to keep Boost or CVODE if they're slower and less
robust?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] buffering output [was [stan-users] RStan multiple parallel instances ...]
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] buffering output [was [stan-users] RStan multiple parallel instances ...]
messages.body_plain:
I think you're the only user at this point, so it's up to you.

Yes, buffering makes a huge difference because it removes
the extra latency per transaction.

How many chains are you running in parallel and how many cores
are you using?  I'd think if there were two threads per chain
being heavily utilized, you'd need eight cores to get decent
performance.

- Bob

> On Apr 4, 2016, at 8:00 AM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Sunday, April 3, 2016 at 3:18:30 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> Thanks for the analysis.  That's really helpful.
>>
>> I would have thought the right transaction granularity (for
>> both semantics and streaming speed) would be a row (iteration) rather
>> than a parameter.
>
> Yes, that is how it is currently implemented.  Sorry if I gave the wrong
> impression.  The other major speed improvement would be to make
> each insert a multi-value insert, but then the class has more complicated
> SQL in it so... tests before optimization.  Apparently (http://www.depesz.com/2007/07/05/how-to-insert-data-to-database-as-fast-as-possible/) multi-value inserts up to 25 or
> so at a time give a really dramatic speed-up (a little over twice?)
>
>> Given that there's per-transaction disk overhead
>> plus handshake latency, this could make a big difference (that'll vary
>> by number of parameters).
>>
>> I've never really worked directly with databases, so don't really
>> know what to expect from throughput.  Inverted indexes for text
>> search are pretty fast to write by comparison (without transactional
>> support).
>>
>> The CSV writer is already slow compared to a binary writer;
>> .3ms per 1K params is 3M double values/second, which is
>> only 24MB/second of raw binary data, which is something like an order of
>> of magnitude under disk throughput.  It's usually the latency of writes
>> that's the killer, with solid states being way better than spinny disks,
>> which are in turn way better than most network storage options.
>
> That's a good reality check.
>
> I'm not really sure how much the SQL writer is worth optimizing really: Even with just
> one worker thread the writer does not slow down Stan and if getting the
> last iterations out of memory and into the DB happens two hours after a six
> hour run... I'm not sure that I care?  Sure it would be nice to avoid but
> the run is available for rough analysis from the database mostly as it's produced.
>
> Krzysztof
>
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>> On Apr 2, 2016, at 10:54 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> On Saturday, April 2, 2016 at 3:57:30 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>>> Yikes.  Is it a very easy Stan model with lots of parameters?
>>>
>>> Once I have it in CmdStan it'll be simpler to see how the two parts work together. I think a model drawing N iterations of K N(0,1) variables per
>>> iteration would be a good test.
>>>
>>>> I'd think you'd want to wrap a buffered commit and make the
>>>> whole thing transactional in order to report back, but wouldn't
>>>> want to commit as you go.  Or is the whole reason you're doing this
>>>> to allow saving intermediate state if something goes wrong?
>>>
>>> I'd like to do this more or less as streaming because I want to see
>>> the output as it's produced.  At the moment one iteration (however
>>> many parameters) is one transaction.  It's actually really fast
>>> for the main thread because the parameters are just copied
>>> copied (as a std::vector<double> into a std::queue<std::vector<double>>
>>> and the main thread moves on (to the next Stan iteration).  The worker threads then take iterations off the queue and now that I've gotten std::chrono figured out it looks like it takes ~1 second per 1,000 parameters CPU time per worker thread.  Since this is 1 insert per parameter it's about on par with what people seem to cite as the kind of performance you get form unoptimized inserts.  It is a little shocking how fast the .csv writer is in comparison (0.3ms for 1,000 parameters with similar instrumentation on the operator()(std::vector<double>))
>>>
>>> I'm thinking of this in the context of a model with ~40k parameters that
>>> takes maybe 8+ hours (?) to run.  With a single worker thread that
>>> would be about 11 hours of time getting everything written into the DB
>>> and no real increase to the Stan run-time---the workers just finish
>>> processing/writing iterations after the sampler is done. With two worker
>>> threads they stay ahead of the sampler.  On a multi-core desktop with 32GB RAM it's really fine.
>>>
>>> I tend to work from a laptop and run Stan on a server/desktop I access from the command line. The second half of the workflow is that I can access Stan output in postgres directly from my laptop with R/dplyr (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dplyr/vignettes/databases.html) without worrying whether I need to move a 500MB csv file or try to read it over a network filesystem.
>>>
>>> There's a moderate size cottage industry (and
>>> slew of stack overflow Q&A) around optimizing writes to postgres
>>> with a lot of good stuff I could use.  The code I wrote is clearly doing some things in the least efficient way possible.  Worst case I could be reducing the write time  quite a bit by writing each iteration as binary to the db and having a trigger that unpacks it on the db side.  Point is, there are lots of ways of optimizing this, but in the meantime it's not looking too bad.
>>>
>>> Krzysztof
>>>
>>>> - Bob
>>>>
>>>>
>>>>> On Apr 1, 2016, at 4:18 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>>
>>>>> On Friday, April 1, 2016 at 3:27:21 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>>>>> Cool!
>>>>>>
>>>>>> The C++11 is the real killer for compatiblity, but that's
>>>>>> less of an issue with CmdStan than anything else.  Especially
>>>>>> if compiling the relevant translation unit is made optional.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> I assume the C++11 is for the thread support.
>>>>>
>>>>> Yeah, once I made the decision to go that route other things probably
>>>>> snuck in but threading is the main thing.
>>>>>
>>>>>> Is postgres slow
>>>>>> enough that it needs a dedicated thread?  Can we still run four
>>>>>> processes for four chains in parallel?  If so, then we'll need
>>>>>> 8 cores to run 4 chains if that postgres thread is really necessary.
>>>>>> If the postgres thread is underutilitized, it might make sense to
>>>>>> just remove the C++11 and threading dependency.  If it's all latency
>>>>>> but the throughput is OK (often the case with network I/O), then it
>>>>>> might make sense to buffer.
>>>>>
>>>>> It's the throughput.  All my (informal) timing was on a dual-core laptop
>>>>> (four "cores") with a solid state disk and the database on the same machine.
>>>>> I wanted to avoid diving into the postgres C library and the libpqxx C++ library
>>>>> has this nice layer that will do transactions wrapped in another layer that checks
>>>>> on connection failures and re-tries anything that fails.  There's probably
>>>>> room for improvement but writing code that's both fast AND resilient to
>>>>> network problems is going to be hard.
>>>>>
>>>>> I tried some informal timings (100 iterations of 1,000 parameters and 100 iterations of
>>>>> 100,000 parameters) and it looks like the on-the-fly munging the writer does
>>>>> along with the postgres writes takes about as much CPU time as running Stan
>>>>> so it's a deal breaker (for me) if they need to share a thread but the current
>>>>> design is that the writer piles work onto a queue and has a thread (or a few) that
>>>>> pick up work and write it.  It'll make sense to do real timing tests once I have
>>>>> this thing in the context of CmdStan and some real models.
>>>>>
>>>>> Krzysztof
>>>>>
>>>>>>
>>>>>> - Bob
>>>>>>
>>>>>>> On Apr 1, 2016, at 3:13 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> On Friday, April 1, 2016 at 1:44:20 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>>>>>>> Is there a proposal for an output format?  We can have
>>>>>>>> more than one output format --- the whole point of the writer
>>>>>>>> interface is to make it easy to adapt to different output
>>>>>>>> formats.
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> Speaking of how easy it is to make output formats: there's a (tested!) postgres writer
>>>>>>> callback (that relies on c++11... and spawns an extra thread to stay out of Stan's way) at
>>>>>>> https://github.com/sakrejda/stan/tree/feature/psql-writer-threaded
>>>>>>> All it takes to initialize it is a string (the standard postgres URI string) so I'm hoping early
>>>>>>> next week to jam it into a CmdStan fork.  Between c++11, std::threads, and postgres
>>>>>>> (libpqxx/libpq) there's no hope of having this in any of the current interfaces but I think
>>>>>>> I can keep up a CmdStan fork.
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> Krzysztof
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> - Bob
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>> On Mar 31, 2016, at 6:32 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:

>>>>>>>>> I wrote and tested a protocol buffers binary writer that's a drop in replacement for the file writer in cmdstan.  The main issue with going further down that road is that we don't have an agreed on output format and I don't want to push it forward and then have to rewrite everything when we agree on a format.

mcmc_writer collects the writer objects to simplify MCMC I/O.
In particular, it grabs the current state of the Markov chain, as
well as the state of the sampler, and writes to the various output
streams (info, error, diagnostic, samples, etc) as necessary.  This
way the MCMC code largely doesn’t need to know about the
writers.

messages.body_plain:
The point of this study was to identify how the CVODES numerical
error affects the MCMC output.  Having the results separated by
chain is really helpful as I think it supports Bob’s hypothesis that
the small differences in the solver output as the tolerances are
varied doesn’t affect the states much but introduces enough variation
to make the RNGs incoherent.  In particular, the variation across
tolerances can be accounted for by the expected MCMC standard
error.

I am not happy with setting the boost/CVODE/CVODES tolerances
around 1e-6 to 1e-8 with the tests requiring 1e-6 or 1e-7 accuracy
compared to analytic solutions.  In particular, Sebastian you should
update the CVODES tests to test for, say, 1e-6 accuracy with
whatever CVODES tolerances achieve this accuracy.  Then we
can merge the CVODES changes once the tests pass.

CVODES can largely replace CVODE, but we should keep the boost
solver in as it is _much_ faster for non stiff problems.  It will be important
to have both until we get a solver that can switch between multiple
approaches like LSODA.

messages.body_plain:
So 1E-6 is the tolerance we take forward, great!

@Michael: I assume you refer to the integrate_ode_cvode_prim_test.cpp and integrate_ode_cvode_grad_rev_test.cpp tests. I will double check again, but at least integrate_ode_cvode_grad_rev_test.cpp does test against an analytical solution at a precision of at least 1E-7.

Moreover, I have ported ALL tests which have been written for CVODE to CVODES and they do pass.

Finally, I have already brought the CVODES branch up-to-date with develop such that these printf patches to CVODE are integrated into CVODES by now.

I fully agree with Michael that we need a non-stiff solver in addition to a stiff solver. This is why I enabled a solver option for the cvodes integrator object which allows to set if a non-stiff (=0) or stiff (=1) solver should be used.

I would like to expose the solver option to the user - should I change the existing integrate_ode_cvode function or add a new one integrate_ode_cvodes? The new function signature would have same arguments as integreate_ode_cvode PLUS the solver integer-argument.

Sebastian

On Tuesday, April 5, 2016 at 10:02:47 PM UTC+2, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> The point of this study was to identify how the CVODES numerical
> error affects the MCMC output.  Having the results separated by
> chain is really helpful as I think it supports Bob’s hypothesis that
> the small differences in the solver output as the tolerances are
> varied doesn’t affect the states much but introduces enough variation
> to make the RNGs incoherent.  In particular, the variation across
> tolerances can be accounted for by the expected MCMC standard
> error.
>
> I am not happy with setting the boost/CVODE/CVODES tolerances
> around 1e-6 to 1e-8 with the tests requiring 1e-6 or 1e-7 accuracy
> compared to analytic solutions.  In particular, Sebastian you should
> update the CVODES tests to test for, say, 1e-6 accuracy with
> whatever CVODES tolerances achieve this accuracy.  Then we
> can merge the CVODES changes once the tests pass.
>
> CVODES can largely replace CVODE, but we should keep the boost
> solver in as it is _much_ faster for non stiff problems.  It will be important
> to have both until we get a solver that can switch between multiple
> approaches like LSODA.
>
> On Apr 5, 2016, at 8:31 PM, Bob Carpenter
>

> > I take it this is CVODES and perfect behavior would
> > be overlayed horizontal lines at the true answer.  So
> > the question is what's good enough?
> >
> > What I'd like is some criterion by which we
> > can make decisions on which of these to keep:
> >
> >   * Boost
> >   * CVODE
> >   * CVODES
> >
> > Asked another way, what does Sebastian need to do to convince
> > everyone that CVODEs should go in?   At that point, is there
> > any reason to keep Boost or CVODE if they're slower and less
> > robust?
> >
> > - Bob

> >> On Apr 5, 2016, at 3:20 PM, Sebastian Weber
> >>

> >> Hi!
> >>
> >> @Krysztof: Great to know that you also have a stake at ODEs.
> >>
> >> From the discussion earlier I figured the quickest thing to do is to repeat the plots I have done, but this time I split by chain which is now color coded. So each color corresponds to the same seed and the same chain id at different values of abs+rel tol passed to the ODE integrator (500 warmup/500 iterations). Note that the seed for the parameters is the same for all runs, only the chain_id varied while the stan_seed is also the same everywhere. Moreover, in the plots I am sending around what is declared in the Stan model as parameter is
> >>
> >> theta, omega, sigma
> >>
> >> The other quantities are derived from these. This time I also include the low precision runs from this morning. I think one can see a threshold which is 1E-2 where inferences seem to be consistently pulled into one direction. For the other abs/rel tolerances, from my view on it, I think it is hard to say anything. For me from 1E-6 (including) and onwards everything looks really ok. messages.body_plain:
See inline.

> On Apr 5, 2016, at 5:26 PM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:

> I fully agree with Michael that we need a non-stiff solver in addition to a stiff solver.

OK, that's good to know.

> This is why I enabled a solver option for the cvodes integrator object which allows to set if a non-stiff (=0) or stiff (=1) solver should be used.

I now see from later email that it's two different solvers
built into CVODES.  Do we have:

   stiff:      CVODES > CVODE
   non-stiff:  CVODES > Boost

If so, I don't see any reason to keep CVODE or the Boost solver.

> I would like to expose the solver option to the user

This is just a stiffness option --- not a direct specification
of solver.

> - should I change the existing integrate_ode_cvode function

I don't want to break backward compatibility unless absolutely
necessary, so we can't change existing function argument structure.
At most you can deprecate integrate_ode_cvode and introduce
something new.

> or add a new one integrate_ode_cvodes?

> The new function signature would have same arguments as integreate_ode_cvode PLUS the solver integer-argument.

How about

   integrate_ode(...)
   integrate_ode_stiff(...)

and we deprecate

  integrate_ode_cvode(...)

and leave open the option to swap in new solvers under the hood (out of
user sight and function naming) later.

I think we'll need to also add a new integrate_ode() with user-defined
tolerances.  So there may be four functions under the hood (stiff/non-stiff,
specify control parameters/default tolerances).

Or do you think we're really going to need to give people a whole host
of options of which solver to use?   In which case we might still want
a default (one without a solver name attached) and we may want to flag
these other instances as unsupported (as in they might go away
in the future).

The primary issue is that we don't want to minimize the dependent pacakges
we have to distribute (including libraries within packages like Boost).

The secondary issue is that we don't want to give users inferior choices as
options, because their tendency will be to try them all if there's more than
one given, especially if they think some might be faster.

- Bob

>>>
>>> If so, I don't see any reason to keep CVODE or the Boost solver.
>>>
>>>> I would like to expose the solver option to the user
>>>
>>> This is just a stiffness option --- not a direct specification
>>> of solver.
>>>
>>>> - should I change the existing integrate_ode_cvode function
>>>
>>> I don't want to break backward compatibility unless absolutely
>>> necessary, so we can't change existing function argument structure.
>>> At most you can deprecate integrate_ode_cvode and introduce
>>> something new.
>>>
>>>> or add a new one integrate_ode_cvodes?
>>>
>>>> The new function signature would have same arguments as integreate_ode_cvode PLUS the solver integer-argument.
>>>
>>> How about
>>>
>>>  integrate_ode(...)
>>>  integrate_ode_stiff(...)
>>>
>>> and we deprecate
>>>
>>> integrate_ode_cvode(...)
>>>
>>> and leave open the option to swap in new solvers under the hood (out of
>>> user sight and function naming) later.
>>>
>>> I think we'll need to also add a new integrate_ode() with user-defined
>>> tolerances.  So there may be four functions under the hood (stiff/non-stiff,
>>> specify control parameters/default tolerances).
>>>
>>> Or do you think we're really going to need to give people a whole host
>>> of options of which solver to use?   In which case we might still want
>>> a default (one without a solver name attached) and we may want to flag
>>> these other instances as unsupported (as in they might go away
>>> in the future).
>>>
>>> The primary issue is that we don't want to minimize the dependent pacakges
>>> we have to distribute (including libraries within packages like Boost).
>>>
>>> The secondary issue is that we don't want to give users inferior choices as
>>> options, because their tendency will be to try them all if there's more than
>>> one given, especially if they think some might be faster.
>>>
>>> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
> On Apr 5, 2016, at 6:43 PM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
> ...

> I will try to benchmark Adams vs RK45 on a few cases to get an opinion on that, but probably you are right in that boost odeint is not needed anymore.

Great.  We can keep the old one for backward compatibility if
we introduce new function names.  At least dependencies on Boost
are header only.

> In what sense do you want to maintain back-ward compatibility? I mean the integrate_ode_cvode function only ever existed on the develop branch.

It was released as part of CmdStan.

> This is why I was thinking it would be ok to change it even now.

So let's just deprecate it rather than change it.

> @Michael: I think Bob meant that CVODES has a built-in non-stiff and a stiff solver. I agree that the terminology is confusing. We have the CVODES solver suite which includes Newton (stiff) and Adams Moulton (non-stiff).
>
> You both were too fast for me in posting (and I am too tired). We are cross-posting.
>
> I can live with that proposal too. Still, I would like to understand at what point you guys consider that we need to maintain back-wards compatibility...

Everything we expose and document should be maintained until we hit
a major version number, the next one of which will be Stan 3 (and
that probably won't arrive for a year, and even then we don't need
to change things so much as deprecate them).

It is really annoying to users to find code not working that
used to work.

I am, on the other hand, OK with removing the doc for things that
are deprecated as long as they still work.

- Bob

Which pull request are we talking about? If we're talking about my pull request to add vectorizing unary functions, I noticed that the functions causing problems are those that:

1) Are untemplated in stan/math/prim/scal/fun and

2) Are externed in math.h (e.g. extern double exp2(double) in math.h)

I tried removing the prim version of exp2 today, but it looks like exp2 becomes part of cmath only for C++11. Also, I think the only other functions with this issue are log2 and log1p, but I can't verify because of a segfault error when testing stan-headers for functions. Those two functions also become part of cmath for C++11.

messages.body_plain:
Rayleigh, here's how to recreate what's going on Jenkins. I was able to recreate it locally.

Hopefully you can follow these steps. I'm going to have you clone two instances of stan so you can keep one on develop.

1. Clone the first instance of Stan:
    git clone https://github.com/stan-dev/stan stan-develop
2. Update the submodules
    cd stan-develop
    git submodule update --recursive --init
    (you might not need recursive since math doesn't have submodules)
3. Run the test that passes on develop:
    make src/test/test-models/good/function-signatures/math/functions/exp2.hpp-test
4. Clone the second instance of Stan:
    git clone https://github.com/stan-dev/stan stan-202
5. Update the submodule
    cd stan-202
    git submodule update --recursive --init
    pushd lib/stan_math
    git checkout feature/issue-202-vectorize-all
    popd
6. Run the test that fails with your branch:
    make src/test/test-models/good/function-signatures/math/functions/exp2.hpp-test

So, you'll notice steps 3 and 6 show the problem.

One last hint to help you find out what's causing the problem: use the -M option on the compiler. If you see the clang++ call for
    make src/test/test-models/good/function-signatures/math/functions/exp2.hpp-test
it's
    clang++ -I src -isystem lib/stan_math/lib/eigen_3.2.8 -isystem lib/stan_math/lib/boost_1.60.0 -isystem lib/stan_math/ -Wall -DBOOST_RESULT_OF_USE_TR1 -DBOOST_NO_DECLTYPE -DBOOST_DISABLE_ASSERTS -pipe -Ilib/stan_math/lib/cvode_2.8.2/include -Wno-unknown-warning-option -Wno-unused-function -Wno-tautological-compare -Wno-c++11-long-long -Wsign-compare -Wno-unused-local-typedef -ftemplate-depth=256   -c -fsyntax-only -O0 src/test/test-models/good/function-signatures/math/functions/exp2.hpp

Add a -M option to that (at the end, after exp2.hpp, is fine). You should see something like:

clang: warning: argument unused during compilation: '-fsyntax-only'
exp2.o: \
  src/test/test-models/good/function-signatures/math/functions/exp2.hpp \
  src/stan/model/model_header.hpp lib/stan_math/stan/math.hpp \
  lib/stan_math/stan/math/rev/mat.hpp \
  lib/stan_math/stan/math/rev/core.hpp \

It's going to be tricky -- I just looked and it's not obvious what's different. You might also want to look at the generated exp2.hpp file. Perhaps we're not generating the C++ in the right way?

Daniel

We can't use C++11 yet.  I thought there were a couple of holdouts.

(1) and (2) are clues enough this should be possible to track down.

Did you mean "or" here?  exp2 is templated in prim/scal/fun/exp2.hpp:

    template <typename T>
    inline typename boost::math::tools::promote_args<T>::type
    exp2(const T y) {
      using std::pow;
      return pow(2.0, y);
    }

I also think these should be const T& not just const T if
they are going to accept var and fvar inputs.

Another hint is that the lib only defines a double version, not
an int version.

C++11 then overloads for integer types with T.  Are you compiling
with C++11 flags on by any chance?

See:  http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/cmath/exp2/

> 2) Are externed in math.h (e.g. extern double exp2(double) in math.h)
>
> I tried removing the prim version of exp2 today,

You can also try defining it for double values instead of having

What do you mean by stan-headers here?  The R package?

We can't use C++11 yet.

messages.subject: precompilation and densities
messages.body_plain:
I've been wondering how big the object file would be
if we precompiled everything in math other than the
densities.

And we might be able to deal with densities for
the most part with this pattern:

  template <typename T, typename U>

  return_type<T, U>::type
  exponential(const T& y, const T& alpha) {

     VectorView<T, ...> y_vec(y);
     VectorView<U, ...> alpha_vec(alpha);

     return exponential_vec(y_vec, alpha_vec);
  }

Then we could precompile exponential_vec for the combos
we need (double, integer, other) where other is var
or fvar<T>, so that's just 3^N for N arguments for reverse
mode (and another 3^N for each other autodiff instantiation).
Still 81 for student-T, but it's not the tens of thousands we
get from all the ways a vector view can be constructed.
Even the VectorView instances can be precompiled here --- there
aren't that many.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I wasn't clear in my last email. I have been able to recreate the issue locally using what you pointed out, Daniel. However, when I try running make src/test/test-models/good/function-signatures/math/functions/exp2.hpp-test after pulling the latest develop version of Stan, I get a segmentation fault error.

As for your question, Bob, I meant and. On the develop branch, exp2 is templated, but on my branch/pull request (issue-202/vectorize-all), it's not in order to vectorize it. From what I remember about the error message, it looked to be failing because extern double exp2(double) in math.h is ambiguous. That call finds two candidate functions: the rev version of exp2 and the untemplated prim version of exp2. When I re-templated exp2 and ran make src/test/test-models/good/function-signatures/math/functions/exp2.hpp-test on Monday, I didn't get an error message. I tried removing the prim version of exp2 as another way to resolve the ambiguity, but as pointed above, I ran into the issue that exp2 is only part of C++11's cmath.

Best,
Rayleigh

>
> Did you mean "or" here?  exp2 is templated in prim/scal/fun/exp2.hpp:

>     inline typename boost::math::tools::promote_args<T>::type
>     exp2(const T y) {
>       using std::pow;
>       return pow(2.0, y);
>     }

> they are going to accept var and fvar inputs.

> Another hint is that the lib only defines a double version, not
> an int version.
>
> C++11 then overloads for integer types with T.  Are you compiling
> with C++11 flags on by any chance?
>
> See:  http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/cmath/exp2/
>
> > 2) Are externed in math.h (e.g. extern double exp2(double) in math.h)

Hi!

I think there is an issue with the nested AD stuff, i.e. the results from the jacobian function are wrong if no stan::math:var instance was initialized before calling the function.

Attached is a cpp file triggering the error and a comment showing how to fix it from the user side. The respective issue is here:

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] math.h vs. cmath
messages.body_plain:
You need to work through this on first principles and
track down where the ambiguity is.  We can help you do
it after the 2.10 release if you haven't figured it out
by then.

I didn't realize you untemplated it.   exp2(double) in math.h isn't
ambiguous by itself.  If it were, nobody would be able to use it!
So something else is being included that causes the ambiguity.
And my guess is that you have the definition in stan::math and
the definition in :: from math.h.  You need to solve this by making
sure both are not brought in.  You can do that in a couple of ways.
It's not critical that we define a primitive version in stan::math.
The one from the library can be included.

All this talk about C++11 is confusing me.  We are NOT moving to
C++11 yet, so we CANNOT introduce dependencies on C++11.  But we
might be testing for C++11 compatibility (I'm not sure any more --- it's
been on and off the table since the project started;  once these
replies get this deep if you want answers, you'll need to dig yourself
or ask someone else --- nobody else is still reading).  If we are
testing for C++11 compatibility, that produces further constraints on
what you can do.

But for now, we MUST bring in a different implementation other than
the C++11 definition, so the question is whether to bring one in
from Boost or by defining one ourselves.  In the past, we've defined
exp2 ourselves.  There's no reason that basic definition needs to
be templated.  It does need to work for int and double.

So what you need to do is track down where the ambiguity is being
brought in.  It's probably from too many using statements, etc.

If you're segfaulting in a test, figure out where by instrumenting
with print statements.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Vectorizing question
messages.body_plain:
> On Apr 6, 2016, at 12:08 PM, Rayleigh L <rayleig...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> While looking through math functions only in C++11 cmath, I noticed that asinh, acosh, and atanh are only available in C++11. So, to vectorize them, I switched to using the boost version of these functions. While asinh passes the tests, acosh and atanh don't because the boost version handles invalid input differently than the rev and fwd versions.

You can write a stan::math version that imports Boost and
handles invalid input consistently.

We haven't been super consistent on handling invalid input
because I was trying to have our autodiff library have the
same invalid input handling as the std lib (that is, log
returns NaN rather than throwing an exception if you
give it a negative input).

> Here's some of the rev mode code for atan (acosh and asinh are similar):
>
> class atanh_vari : public op_v_vari {
>
>       public:
>
>         atanh_vari(double val, vari* avi) :
>
>           op_v_vari(val, avi) {
>
>         }
>
>         void chain() {
>
>           avi_->adj_ += adj_ / (1.0 - avi_->val_ * avi_->val_);
>
>         }
>
>       };
>
>
>
> and some of the fwd mode code for atanh (acosh and asinh are similar):
>
>
>
> template <typename T>
>
>     inline fvar<T> atanh(const fvar<T>& x) {
>
>       using ::atanh;
>
>       using stan::math::square;
>
>       return fvar<T>(atanh(x.val_), x.d_ / (1 - square(x.val_)));
>
>
>     }
>
>
>
> Shouldn't they use the boost version throughout all modes? If so, should I create an issue for this?

Yes, they should ideally be using the same implementation.
And they should have behavior consistent with the std:: library,
at least for now and at least where possible.

It's a huge pain, but you have to learn how to debug yourself.
It took Daniel and I a long time for C++ and you can see we're
still spending a huge amount of time trying to help you on this
one issue (though it's really a bunch of little issues).

The design's another issue, like what our error behavior should
be --- please do keep bringing these issues up.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Feather (re: output format)
messages.body_plain:
> On Apr 6, 2016, at 4:12 PM, Allen B. Riddell <a...@ariddell.org> wrote:
>
> I can't imagine the Hadoop/Spark/etc people don't have a way of dealing
> with this problem (streaming data). It would be interesting to find out
> what it is.

The underlying C++ interfaces we're building do stream.  What
we're really talking about are:

 * a data serialization scheme

 * persistence mechanism

These are often be tied together, as with a database scheme
and database transactional storage.

This all has to live on top of a

 * transport layer

That can just be file streams on a desktop or SSL over the
network.  As soon as we talk network, there's also a

 * security layer

Tools like Hadoop/Spark are mainly about a networked transport layer
(and job control), though often interface with network file systems
or databases for persistence.  They're very flexible because they
don't build many assumptions in, but just get out of the way and let
you stream bytes.

There are probably good practices for organizing said stream
of bytes, but I don't know much about it other than what I
can work out from first principles (like buffering over networks).

I think this is all worth thinking about.  We've talked about
it before when someone wanted to do JSON output, which is where
the by-row vs. by-column discussion came up.

Protocol buffers seem to make a lot of sense if we can overcome
the size limitations (which don't seem that limiting) and they
scale well as overall size increases.

- Bob

Hi!

So we are going to bring in CVODES into Stan as far as I understood. To go forward I will

1. open issues on stan and cmdstan (rstan?)

1. Being able to remove the integrate_ode_cvode function now, i.e. we would not have to carry around a deprecated function
2. We only have to deal with changeing libraries once for the interfaces
3. Very likely more happy ODE users (certainly my models will run *much* faster)

Best,
Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
For reference:

The bulk of the CVODES code is in the files under stan/math/rev/arr/functor/:

- integrate_ode_cvodes.hpp : user-facing function
- cvodes_integrator.hpp : CVODES integrator interface
- ode_model.hpp : helper object to get easily the Jacobian of the ODE RHS function wrt to states and parameters
- decouple_states.hpp : helper which takes output from cvodes_integrator and creates with precomputed_gradient the output for integrate_ode_cvodes

The helper objects I had to introduce as I needed the mathematical objects a bit more granular than I would get it from the coupled_ode_system. It would make sense in going forward to refactor the coupled_ode_model object implementation using the two helpers I introduced, but that can be done at a later stage.

Sebastian

1) clone the github repository
2) manually follow the instructions at https://github.com/wesm/feather/blob/master/R/configure
2a) make the new subdirectories under /R/src
2b) copy the feather and flatbuffer files from src to R/src/feather etc.
2c) It seems that the tests are no longer in src (see https://github.com/wesm/feather/commit/fa0d80caf3ea3866586972da26035e3c44d2529e ). If they are there, delete them
3) build package from source

Then you should have a working feather installation.

Avi

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

This came up in the meeting today. Here is the current status:
Issue: https://github.com/stan-dev/math/issues/191
 <https://github.com/stan-dev/math/issues/191>Feature branch (on math): https://github.com/stan-dev/math/tree/feature/issue-191-gp-squared_exponential

If anyone wants to help, we need to add tests for derivatives in rev, fwd, and mix for the function. The implementation should be complete now.

To add this to the Stan language, it's going to be straightforward. We just need to add these function signatures:
1. matrix cov_sq_exp(real[], real, real)
2. matrix cov_sq_exp(vector[], real, real)
3. matrix cov_sq_exp(row_vector[], real, real)
4. matrix cov_sq_exp(matrix[], real, real)
5. matrix cov_sq_exp(real[], real[], real, real)
6. matrix cov_sq_exp(vector[], vector[], real, real)
7. matrix cov_sq_exp(row_vector[], row_vector[], real, real)
8. matrix cov_sq_exp(matrix[], matrix[], real, real)

I just want to make sure it's tested under those signatures in the math library before propagating all the way through to develop. After tests are in, we can do some custom gradients instead of relying on autodiff.

Also, I had been thinking about extending for:
- sigma: real[]
- length scale: real[] or vector or matrix.
But, I want to wait for the first implementation to go out.

Daniel

messages.subject: new ODE functions
messages.body_plain:
[off issue]

We need to add the stiff ODE solver to the language, and so
need a name.

A.  Current proposal is for four functions with two names (the
control params being optional):

   integrate_ode_cvodes(...args..., ...control params...)
   integrate_ode_cvodes_stiff(...args..., ...control params...);

B.  An alternative, which I prefer, would be to drop "cvodes" from
the name and just go with

   integrate_ode(...)
   integrate_ode_stiff(...)

We'd then replace the Boost solver currently behind integrate_ode
with the CVODES non-stiff solver.   Note that we don't name other
functions with the packages providing algorithms used to compute them!
But I seem to recall some issue with efficiency.  Is the non-stiff
CVODES solver just overall better rthan the Runge-Kutta implementation
in Boost?

C.  Add in the algorithm name, rather than implementation pacakge:

  integrate_ode_adams_moulton(...)

and so on.  I don't even know what these are, but they might be more
familiar to users than "cvodes".

Any preferences?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: new ODE functions
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I agree that the specific implementation (CVODES) is not so of interest to the user. I am suggesting a blend of the above:

- we have two simple go-to default functions for users:

  integrate_ode  => non-stiff
  integrate_ode_stiff   => stiff

  These functions set the default abs+rel tol and maximum number of steps.

- Additionally, we have functions with more control which are named for their algorithm:

  integrate_ode_rk45
  integrate_ode_adams_moulton
  integrate_ode_bdf

  These functions would take extra arguments for abs+rel tol and maximum number of steps.

This way we would have covered expert users and normal mortals. This would also be in line with what I see in other ODE packages, i.e. they make the options named after the algorithm.

I would prefer to keep the rk45 from boost in addition to the adams_moulton from CVODES. The material is far to complex for me to exhaustively cover this with benchmark tests to decide which one is really better and I do think this will actually always depend on the exact model, etc.. RK45 is around for ages as is adams_moulton. Moreover, adams_moulton is advertised as requiring fewer calls to the ODE RHS and the sensitivity ODE RHS. From that angle adams_moulton should be better than RK45, since it avoids a few calls to AD.

If you think getting rid of boost odeint is a big advantage, then so be it.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: new ODE functions
messages.body_plain:
I like your proposal

>  integrate_ode  => non-stiff
>  integrate_ode_stiff   => stiff
>
>  These functions set the default abs+rel tol and maximum number of steps.
>
> - Additionally, we have functions with more control which are named for their algorithm:
>
>  integrate_ode_rk45
>  integrate_ode_adams_moulton
>  integrate_ode_bdf

There are sizeable advantages to having fewer functions for both
users and developers.

For users, there's much less to read and many fewer decisions to
make, so much less chance of being overwhelmed by detail or being
tempted into trying all the options. Of course, this only makes sense if expert
users don't need to make those decisions.

On the dev side, fewer functions and code dependencies means
proportionally less doc, testing, and ongoing maintenance.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: new ODE functions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob!

Hmm... your arguments make sense. Also, thinking about how much code could go away if we remove the odeint RK45 integrator...that's quite a lot of code+testing code. From that perspective going with CVODES only is a big win, true. Ok, even though this won't cover everything I will fire off tomorrow a benchmark for a non-stiff problem which takes 2-3 days. That is a good stress test for the Adams-Moulton and the RK45 integrator.

And 4 variants of integrate_ode are easier to read than using algorithms name for the advanced functions, also agreed. I only think that this naming scheme is not really expandable (and only experts use it, so it's fine to have the names), but maybe that is just a minor point. As I have been exposed to these things so much, I like my details; but maybe they don't matter so much in the end. Bottom line: I can live with your option A.

Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stan ODE paper?
messages.body_plain:
I hate to admit if Stan is not good at something, but ODEs have definetly not been a strong field for Stan up till now. That is, Stan oftentimes just ran against the wall by freezing the boost odeint integrator. With the robust RK45 patch and CVODES this is history.

I am happy to file a PK/PD example soon with the shiny new CVODES integrator.

Sebastian

but I’m not sure how to properly include the higher-order autodiff.  To see
the current compiler errors you can run the broken test in stan-dev/stan,

make clean-all
git checkout feature/issue-304-add_rhmc
./runTests.py src/test/unit/mcmc/hmc/hamiltonians/softabs_metric_test.cpp

If anyone wants to peruse the implementation of the SoftAbs metric in
src/stan/mcmc/hmc/hamiltonians/softabs_metric.hpp I would also be
appreciative.  I’m trying not to prematurely optimize, but Riemannian
HMC is going to use a lot more memory so there will likely be lots of
improvements to the code.  For reference the analytical equations are
all in http://arxiv.org/abs/1212.4693.
