messages.subject: Scripting help.
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I could use your help with some scripting help.

When the math library's develop branch changes (github.com/stan-dev/math <http://github.com/stan-dev/math>), I have Jenkins run a script to update the upstream project, Stan (github.com/stan-dev/stan <http://github.com/stan-dev/stan>). This is the current script: https://github.com/syclik/stan-scripts/blob/master/jenkins/create-stan-pull-request.sh

Here's the current flow. It starts when math's develop branch is changed.

0. (Local) Checkout stan-dev/stan and update to develop. Change directories into that directory.
1. (Local) Check to see if the math branch has actually changed. If not, don't do anything.
2. (GitHub) Create a github issue with title "Update submodule for the Stan Math Library". Save the issue number.
3. (Local) Create a new feature branch named feature/issue-#-update-math where # is the issue number.
4. (Local) Update the math submodule to develop. Stage the change to the submodule. Commit. Push to the remote.
5. (GitHub) Create a pull request with the feature branch.

What would be ideal is a check to see if an issue exists with the title "Update submodule for the Stan Math Library" it would then update the existing feature branch. No need to create a new pull request. Perhaps a new comment.

Help? I tried doing it, but I'm not that great at scripting.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Let's discuss this at the meeting Tuesday and see if
everyone else is OK getting rid of Boost's odeint and
just going with CVODES.

No matter what we do with function names, the details
of what's going on under the hood will be available.
I think it's critical to make the high-level code to
lower-level code path as transparent as possible for
power users --- it's the only way to write good code
in a language, be it C++ or Stan or R.

From that perspective going with CVODES only is a big win, true. Ok, even though this won't cover everything I will fire off tomorrow a benchmark for a non-stiff problem which takes 2-3 days. That is a good stress test for the Adams-Moulton and the RK45 integrator.
>

I only think that this naming scheme is not really expandable (and only experts use it, so it's fine to have the names), but maybe that is just a minor point. Hi!

I have done now a bit of benchmarking and from this I can say that RK45 is 3-5x FASTER in comparison to the Adams-Moulton from CVODES! So I would definitely recommend to keep RK45.

In order to double check that my approaches with ode_model (used in the Adams-Moulton) etc. is not the root cause for the slow down I also went ahead an reimplemented the odeint integrator with these building blocks. The speed of this newly implemented odeint RK45 integrator is the same as the old one. The nice thing though is that I can cut down on lines of code from ~800 to ~300 and out of the ~300 about 200 come from ode_model and decouple_ode_states. Hence, I would recommend to refactor the old code with these pieces, but surely keep RK45.

I have the code written, but as it depends on pieces in the CVODES branch, can I just branch of that one?

Sebastian

(I ran the new RK45 code with the existing tests for odeint and all were good)

The benchmarks I did apply to my test case (2cmt oral PK model). I would recommend (in order of importance):

1. Keep integrate_ode with the RK45 for non-stiff

We still need to decide of how to name those functions; to be discussed Tuesday?

Sebastian

Hi Daniel!

To clarify what point 2: Yesterday we merge a replacement of the CVODE library with CVODES library, not more. So for stiff problems the integrate_ode_cvode function is still using the old approach of exposing the coupled_ode system to the cvode ode solver, but ignoring the extra capeabilities of CVODES. So for stiff there is still a huge gain by switching to integrate_ode_cvodes.

@ Krzysztof: I don't have this benchmark in a repo yet. I guess I should clean the code and put it onto github, you are right.

Sebastian

messages.subject: Tagged Versions Naming Convention
messages.body_plain:
If I checkout a tagged version of Stan I get library folders named
after each commit.  For example, if I go to cmdstan and

git checkout v2.9.0
git submodule update —init —recursive

then I get the Stan library folder

stan_2.9.0.

The makefile points to the tagged library so everything should
work fine, but it’s confusing to have two Stan libraries around,
the tagged version and the regular “stan” folder that is carried
over from develop, no?

Moreover, when moving back to develop the tagged submodules
won’t be deleted because of their recursive nature (stan_2.9.0
can’t be deleted because it contained a tagged math library).
This has caused me no end of confusion this afternoon when
trying to do a regression test.

I don’t remember this behavior occurring previously — what is
the motivation?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Tagged Versions Naming Convention
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael,

On Sun, Apr 17, 2016 at 1:14 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> If I checkout a tagged version of Stan I get library folders named
> after each commit.  For example, if I go to cmdstan and
>
> git checkout v2.9.0
> git submodule update —init —recursive
>
> then I get the Stan library folder
>
> stan_2.9.0.
>
> The makefile points to the tagged library so everything should
> work fine, but it’s confusing to have two Stan libraries around,
> the tagged version and the regular “stan” folder that is carried
> over from develop, no?

The tagged version, v2.9.0, only points to stan_2.9.0 and not to stan. The "stan" folder you have left over when you check out that particular tag is due to git's conservative nature. In a perfect world, git would remove the "stan" folder and only leave "stan_2.9.0".

>
> Moreover, when moving back to develop the tagged submodules
> won’t be deleted because of their recursive nature (stan_2.9.0
> can’t be deleted because it contained a tagged math library).
> This has caused me no end of confusion this afternoon when
> trying to do a regression test.

The same goes the other way.

>
> I don’t remember this behavior occurring previously — what is
> the motivation?

There were a few reasons for doing this -- I'm not sure any of them are really good reasons for continuing to do it:
- debugging users' configuration. Our initial concern was users substituting submodule branches and the developers chasing down bugs on stale branches. We haven't had many discussions on the stan-users list with users doing this, so it's not really a good reason.
- quick inspection and knowing what version we're looking at.
....

I thought there were more reasons, but I can't think of any right now. We thought more users would swap out branches and we'd spend time trying to find out what's going on when it's not really a Stan problem but with configuration. It just lives like that for a couple commits at each tag, but we don't have to do it that way. It would make tracking through the commits a little better. We already do some special things now when we tag which includes building the manual and checking that in so it's part of the distribution. I'm not sure how many people actually like having the user manual distributed in the tarball, but we could remove that too.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

My benchmarks tests are somewhat specialized to our computing environment. So I use a system like

1. An R script which sets up simulated data, inits and everything else what is needed to kick off a Stan run. This is the "model" file as I call it.

2. Another R script which takes the model file, parses it, creates a sub-directory, serializes the data into that directory, copies the stan source and executable into it, sets up init files and finally creates "fit.sh" and optionally "post.sh".

3. then I submit things into the SGE cluster queue

However, the script fit.sh can be called from the command line like

./fit.sh

(trivial). This will start chain id 1; if you want chain X then you do

SGE_TASK_ID=X ./fit.sh

Is that too "local" or would that suffices to linger in one of the stan repos?

Sebastian

Putting things into the stan github raises the bar a bit for me - I don't always go forward with clean code (although I put quite some tests in my code) and before I share code some polishing should be done...

messages.body_plain:
Hi Daniel,

First, I think the issue+pull approach is great for most stuff! Still, I find myself not fixing one-liners just due to the hassle of going through the process. So maybe a process for "small" fixes could be added to the processes. Here are two ideas:

1. We all agree that leaving those templates which we have in most parts empty if a change is small is ok.

2. Each developer keeps an open branch for small fixes. Each commit to that branch must only be a small change and should be accompanied by a descriptive commit message. Once the developer reaches a threshold (maybe 5) of such small commits, he creates an issue+pull which lists those small changes.

Finally, we would need to define what "small" is. One-liners, removing compiler warnings, etc. ... needs to be defined on a wiki.

I think this would help to make small changes go in quicker.

Just an idea.

Sebastian

messages.subject: My development activity after v2.10.0
messages.body_plain:
0. I'm looking forward to tagging Math v2.10.0 and Stan v2.10.0. We should be able to tag both asap. We are currently waiting on 1 thing:
  - Math: review of a pull request that fixes the binomial_coefficient_log bug from rstan:: https://github.com/stan-dev/math/pull/273

Michael's implementation of the stiff solver will be in the next release. I haven't looked at how that's exposed through the language. I think we should look at that before v2.10.0 is released since I think we have a clearer idea of how we want to expose the integrate_ode_* functions in the language. We've already swapped out CVODE for CVODES here.

Sebastian's new stiff solver implementation will not be in the next release. It needs a bit more work and I need to review the tests. I haven't even checked to see if it's instantiated in the ways Stan would instantiate it.

1. After v2.10.0, the core libraries are going to move around. Right now we have two core libraries:
- Stan: stan-dev/stan
- Math: stan-dev/math

Stan is now going to be split into language, algorithms, services. I forget if we decided to abbreviate or not, but it should look like:
- language: stan-dev/language
- algorithms: stan-dev/algorithms
- services: stan-dev/services
- math: stan-dev/math

There are two main concerns I have: 1) making it easy on the developers and 2) keep some sort of history and leave the builds relatively intact.

I think if we renamed the stan-dev/stan repo, GitHub will help us out and track the submodule through the name change. I think stan-dev/stan should be renamed to stan-dev/language and we can copy the repos into algorithms and services.

Questions:
- if we wanted to do abbreviations, what should they be? lang, alg, api?
- should stan-dev/stan be renamed to algorithms instead of language?

Any major objections? This will take a little bit of work, but I think it's for the best. Here's how the dependencies will work:

rstan/pystan/cmdstan -> services  ->  algorithms  -> math
                                  ->  language

Math won't need to be touched. (Sebastian and Rayleigh, this means the work you're doing won't be affected at all.)

Mike, hopefully this doesn't mess up your world. If you've pushed to branches, I can try to move all the branches over. That make sense to you?

2. Full logging instead of streams.
Once we break apart the Stan repo, we can then implement full logging with logging levels. See https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Consolidated-Output-for-Sample,-Optimize,-ADVI,-and-Diagnose

This means we can be consistent with our output from the core library and we can use structured output so rstan's output can be controlled easily.

This will also help Krzysztof with what he's implementing with databases and other outputs.

3. Services. This is the biggie. This will take most of the duplicated code out of cmdstan, rstan, and pystan.

(Mike, you were right about having a consolidated config. The implementation wasn't and I was too caught up in the details. Bob sketched out something that will work. I can implement it cleanly and I want to push so this can happen very quickly.)

I'm pretty sure I know how all the pieces fit, so I'm ready to move forward and replace everything. The overall interfaces won't change, but the backend will be a lot easier to manage.

Any objections? Any suggestions? Anyone want to help?

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: unit scale! [moved from stan-users]
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Ahh... now I get it. Not really, I did not code the constrained ones, i.e. I had some standard deviations which were coded on log-space, but then I anyway used a prior on the log-scale.

Good modeling practice is to go to unconstrained in any case. There are models where this is hard and I love in these cases the clever tricks Stan does in the background for me. So this feature is dangerous for some of those involved types, yes. I missed your discussion around this and the rationale for not doing it, sorry.

However, having done this type of programming - I don't see a big problem in letting people do this themselves. Moreover, this way I can leave the variables which are anyway at unit-scale (Matt trick) as they are and I don't mess around with them. So maybe this feature is not so badly needed...

Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] My development activity after v2.10.0
messages.body_plain:
There are several pieces to the new interface design:

  readers
  writers
  services

The services are the facade for the algorithms like NUTS and L-BFGS
(I think that's what Michael and Daniel have been calling
"routes", but I'm not 100% sure).  The services involve readers and
writers as callbacks.  They shouldn't require any Boost or Eigen data
structures.

The services design will be very similar to Michael's
original plan in its client-facing API.

I don't know if there are any Eigen types left in the readers/writers.

Sticking to C++ is easy for 1D containers, but not so
good for 2D structures.  But most (all?) of those are going to be
encapsulated in the readers/writers (I don't think user-supplied
mass matrices will land in the first version).

We won't be moving to C++11 until our interfaces can
cope.

We'll still need Boost and Eigen on the back end.

- Bob

messages.subject: Writers in the HMC Code
messages.body_plain:
I just spend the last there hours or so trying to incorporate all of the
changes needed to make the RHMC branch work with the added
error writers, and not the majority of the HMC code is passing around
these f’ing writers, most of which do nothing.  When more writers
are added to implement logging it’s going to get even worse.

I really want to fix this soon to put the HMC code back in a clean
state.  I imagine this would consist of

a) A logger object which wraps all of the necessary writers and
    exposes methods like “write_info”, “writer_fatal”, etc.

b) Passing the logger to the samplers on construction.

c) Storing a reference to the input logger in the internal ps_point
    instantiation so that when this->z_ is passed around so to is
    the logger.

In this way the logging implementation can be tweaked without
affecting the HMC code.

Also, in the future please don’t merge updates that touch nearly
all of the HMC code without my review.

messages.body_plain:
Whatever happens, you (Allen) are in charge of the PyStan repo,
so you should use your own judgment and use GitHub however
you see fit.

My own preference is

  * email for starting a discussion,

  * Wiki for a design/API doc,

  * a branch for the code, which you can use to get feedback
    on the coding, and

  * a pull request when it's ready to be merged and just
    needs a final code review.

It's a very ad hoc process, but GitHub's not really set
up to do all of those things well.  Lots of people manage this
process separately in other software.

I like the Wiki at the design stage because you can edit it
to be up to date and don't have to try to infer the design
goals from the code.

- Bob

messages.subject: ODE matters
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

with the cvodes implementation I introduced what I called the ode_model class. This class binds together what I think belongs together in this context. The class will allow us to cut down existing code, make the ODE code more readable and it will also easily enable the use of analytic Jacobians with ODEs at some point (such that AD is avoided). Please find attached a PDF which lays out my thinking.

Comments are very welcome. Throughout the current cvodes pull request it was moreover suggested to rename the ode_model class into ode only. My motivation to call this class more than just ode is that the class encapsulates more than only the ODE RHS, but all additional stuff like Jacobians. So proposals for names are

- ode_model
- ode
- ode_system
- other???

Any input on this would be great. Thanks!

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ODE matters
messages.body_plain:
ode_system is a great name, I will adjust.

Let me explain in more detail, how this is supposed to work. So the ode_system has a declaration like

template<typename F>
ode_system {
ode_system(F model, std::vector<double> theta, ...other stuff to call RHS...)

void operator()(t, y, dy_dt) => calls the functor F to get the ODE RHS

void jacobian_S(t,y,dy_dt,Jy) => calculates the Jacobian wrt to states

void jacobian_SP(t,y,dy_dt,Jy,Jtheta) => calculates the Jacobian wrt to states and parameters

};

So the ode_system is templated by the ODE RHS functor F. Our ODE integrators then use an instance of ode_system<ODE_to_be_solved> in their code. The generic implementation would use auto-diff to get the Jacobians. In case we want to specify analytic Jacobians, then all what would need to be done is define some where a

ode_system<hard_stiff_ODE> {

... definition of ODE RHS ...
... analytic definitions of Jacobian functions ...

};

And then the integrators would use fully analytic Jacobians instead of auto-diff.

An implementation can be found here (I still need to rename):

https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/feature/issue-262-CVODES-2/stan/math/rev/mat/functor/ode_model.hpp

I have tried this approach and it works nicely. For systems where it makes sense to provide the analytic Jacobians, you get 2-3x speedup. Moreover, there are code-generation toolboxes out there which start off with SBML (XML language to describe ODEs) and give you code-generated C++ sources with analytic Jacobians.

I hope that makes sense.

Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
I'm late to the party, but a few comments below:

> Stan is now going to be split into language, algorithms, services. I forget if we decided to abbreviate or not, but it should look like:
>
> - language: stan-dev/language
>
> - algorithms: stan-dev/algorithms
>
> - services: stan-dev/services
>
> - math: stan-dev/math
>

Completely agree this will be helpful and I like the long names. To avoid drowning in multiple issues per real issue, I wonder if we could keep stan-dev/stan as the place where overarching issues with checklists live that need pull requests across all the interfaces.

> 2. Full logging instead of streams.
>
> Once we break apart the Stan repo, we can then implement full logging with logging levels. See https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Consolidated-Output-for-Sample,-Optimize,-ADVI,-and-Diagnose

+1 for key-value output rather than trying a more complex structure.  I guess the middle road would be a lightweight structure that makes it easy for interfaces to check whether a key is available.

> This means we can be consistent with our output from the core library and we can use structured output so rstan's output can be controlled easily.
>
>
> This will also help Krzysztof with what he's implementing with databases and other outputs.

Even now the writer interface is really good.  I think the remaining problems are that output isn't sent to a clear part of the interface (e.g.-something that looks like a key-value message is sent all in one string, something that's just a string is pre-pended with spaces for formatting in a text file, etc...)

>
> 3. Services. This is the biggie. This will take most of the duplicated code out of cmdstan, rstan, and pystan.
>
>
> (Mike, you were right about having a consolidated config. The implementation wasn't and I was too caught up in the details. Bob sketched out something that will work. I can implement it cleanly and I want to push so this can happen very quickly.)
>
>
> I'm pretty sure I know how all the pieces fit, so I'm ready to move forward and replace everything. The overall interfaces won't change, but the backend will be a lot easier to manage.
>
>
>
>
>
> Any objections?

Nope.

> Any suggestions?
> Anyone want to help?

Yep, I had a good conversation with Bob at NESS about how to manage my involvement better.  The specific list I could help on is something like: 1) pulling CmdStan through this process; 2) anything with the writers; 3) taking the current output spec you link to and proposing a key-value version; 4) replacing the reader(s) once we have a solid output spec; and 5) code review on any of the above.

Krzysztof

more descriptive.

valid in this setting?

the naming right.

messages.subject: Rao-Blackwellized HMC
messages.body_plain:
One of the immediate generalizations of algorithms like the No-U-Turn
sampler is to average over the entirety of each trajectory, effectively
Rao-Blackwellizing the algorithm.  I had hesitated implementing this
for a long time because intuitively I didn’t think there could be much
gained if we’re already generating nearly-independent samples.  With
more motivation from the integration time paper that I put out a few
months ago I finally got around to playing with it, and it looks like my
intuitions were largely correct.

Given the marginal improvements I wasn’t planning on putting together
a full paper or anything.

My thoughts:

- interface_callback::writer should stay separate from a logger.  It's a really straightforward interface and works well in the context of messages and other output.
- I don't think we need to decide whether a logger wraps interface_callbacks::writer.  If I were implementing a logger for an interface I might do it that way but at the stan-dev/services level I don't know what would work best.  One thing we get by assuming that the logger wraps interface_callbacks::writer is that we automatically know what kind of output can get sent to the logger and that should simplify defining the interface consistently at the services level.
- If we do wrap interface_callbacks::writer then logger::level() could just do its bit (add timestamp/etc...) and pass the arguments on to a writer.
- I like the function call format (if we wrap writers in the logger) because it makes it clear how they are being called.  I don't have a strong opinion on it.
- If we want to (and I think we do) abstract out the "files vs. terminals vs. elsewhere" issue I think we should stick with wrapping interface_callbacks_writer since that interface already lets us abstract out the issue.

At the c++/CmdStan level it's easy to imagine constructing a logger from the usual stuff---filenames/streams/etc... to echo Bob's question, what do the other interfaces need to be able to send output to?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Rao-Blackwellized HMC
messages.body_plain:
How are you measuring computational cost in plot (d)?  Is that wall-clock time or gradient evaluations or ?  The reason I ask is two fold.  First the time spent computing the gradient for a Gaussian is going to be negligible because of the simple form of the posterior and heavy optimization that's been done for a multivariate normal.  The second is that Stan's I/O (rendering floating point values into plain text) is pretty inefficient and dramatically increasing the number of samples that need to be kept is going to bog things down.  (How much will also depend heavily on whether you're on a SSD, HDD or a networked disk.)  I think showing both (c) and (d) relative to number of gradient evaluations provides a more relevant measure of computational effort than either number of transitions or wall clock time.

Tangentially, Radford proposed this a while back as part of [1] (See section 6 and reference [5] therein) and found some significant benefits to basic HMC.  Also interesting, was that you don't need to use the same weights which are used in the Markov transition kernel for selecting states from the trajectory.  This could, for instance, allow you to store only subsets of the simulated trajectory and reduce the I/O cost.

Cheers,
Marcus

[1] Neal, R. M. (1994). An improved acceptance procedure for the hybrid Monte Carlo algorithm. Journal of Computational Physics, 111:194–203.

messages.body_plain:
I'm also curious how you're doing it, because I wouldn't think
the combination overhead would be too onerous in either time or
memory.

If you're only saving the averages per iteration, there's
the issue of how we deal with the interfaces and whether it'll
be possible to compute proper posterior intervals.

I think there's a lot of possiblity for online algorithms.
For instance, if you're just doing Rao-Blackwell and you want
to normalize, that is you get a stream of

  w[n], p[n]

and you want to compute a weighted average

  sum(w .* p) / sum(w)

then you can do it all with two accumulators on the log scale:

  log(sum(w .* p) / sum(w))

  = log(sum(w .* p)) - log(sum(w))

  = log_sum_exp(log(w) .+ log(p)) - log_sum_exp(log(w))

But to compute p% quantiles, we'd need to save p% of the draws.
Or perhaps we could get a noisier estimate with subsampling (does
the inverse of Rao-Blackwell have a name?).

- Bob

> On Apr 27, 2016, at 12:19 PM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> How are you measuring computational cost in plot (d)?  Is that wall-clock time or gradient evaluations or ?  The reason I ask is two fold.  First the time spent computing the gradient for a Gaussian is going to be negligible because of the simple form of the posterior and heavy optimization that's been done for a multivariate normal.  The second is that Stan's I/O (rendering floating point values into plain text) is pretty inefficient and dramatically increasing the number of samples that need to be kept is going to bog things down.  (How much will also depend heavily on whether you're on a SSD, HDD or a networked disk.)  I think showing both (c) and (d) relative to number of gradient evaluations provides a more relevant measure of computational effort than either number of transitions or wall clock time.

> Tangentially, Radford proposed this a while back as part of [1] (See section 6 and reference [5] therein) and found some significant benefits to basic HMC.  Also interesting, was that you don't need to use the same weights which are used in the Markov transition kernel for selecting states from the trajectory.  This could, for instance, allow you to store only subsets of the simulated trajectory and reduce the I/O cost.
>
> Cheers,
> Marcus
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Rao-Blackwellized HMC
messages.body_plain:
> How are you measuring computational cost in plot (d)?  Is that wall-clock time or gradient evaluations or ?

Wall clock time for running Stan, not for the additional post processing to compute expectations and the like.

> The reason I ask is two fold.  First the time spent computing the gradient for a Gaussian is going to be negligible because of the simple form of the posterior and heavy optimization that's been done for a multivariate normal.  The second is that Stan's I/O (rendering floating point values into plain text) is pretty inefficient and dramatically increasing the number of samples that need to be kept is going to bog things down.  (How much will also depend heavily on whether you're on a SSD, HDD or a networked disk.)  I think showing both (c) and (d) relative to number of gradient evaluations provides a more relevant measure of computational effort than either number of transitions or wall clock time.

None of this is going to matter in practice.  Even if all of the I/O overhead could be avoided, the improvements
are marginal.

> Tangentially, Radford proposed this a while back as part of [1] (See section 6 and reference [5] therein) and found some significant benefits to basic HMC.  Also interesting, was that you don't need to use the same weights which are used in the Markov transition kernel for selecting states from the trajectory.  This could, for instance, allow you to store only subsets of the simulated trajectory and reduce the I/O cost.

The improvements Radford saw were only in comparison to an HMC algorithm that takes the final point of
the trajectory.  Uniformly sampling from the trajectory provides the significant improvement, and then
averaging over the entire trajectory yields only a marginal improvement.

You can use different weights but you still have to ensure the correct marginal probabilities or else you’ll
bias the expectations.  In particular, any subsampling would have to include random decisions as to which
states to keep which reduces the efficacy of the Rao-Blackwellization.

Because I used the marginal probabilities exactly, this is the best that you’re going to do.

[off issue, as this is more general]

> On Apr 27, 2016, at 6:09 AM, Michael Betancourt <notifi...@github.com> wrote:
>
> Many of the comments have been addressed. The only things that I didn't change were
>
> 	• I will get violent about having arguments aligned, even at the expensive of an extra vertical line. This will all go away once we have a decent logger, anyways.

My preference is the other way, but this isn't a big deal.  Our code
format's not that well defined.  We clearly differ tremendously in
our utility function for stretching programs vertically.

...

> 	• You can take my static_cast<double>s from my cold, dead hands. 😁 I can never remember which languages promote in which ways,
> so I tend to err on the side of being too conservative.

The usual code convention is to let the language do its thing
and not add extra annotation for readers who don't know the language.
And that goes for doc, too --- Google even says so explicitly in their
C++ style guide!  That is, it's usual to prefer

  a * b + c

to

 (a * b) + c

and to prefer

  int x;
  double y = 2.0 * x;

to

  int x;
  double y = 2.0 * static_cast<double>(x);

At least you're not static-casting to var, which would be a performance hit.

> I'll keep this in mind if they pop up in the source code.
>
> In the future we should think about the virtual modifiers in base_hamiltonian.hpp. I had them there to define pure virtual methods to enforce an interface, but it might be fruitful to remove them to sacrifice enforcement for performance.

The only reason to have virtual functions is if you are going
to have references to the base class as arguments (i.e., you're
using object oriented programming).  Otherwise, it's just a useless
performance hit.  The compiler will let you know if you're missing pieces
of a necessary concept.

- Bob

In the note I linked to the branch with the implementation.
so you can see all the details directly.

But online won’t work because expectations don’t commute
with nonlinear transformations.  In particular, the trajectories
are in the unconstrained space so we have to constrains the
states (and run generated quantities!) _before_ averaging
the states together, and the code isn’t factored in any way
to do that.

Then there’s the additional problem that you’d have to do
this separately for _every expectation that you want to compute_.
That includes means and variances, but not quantiles as
quantile estimators really aren’t amenable to Rao-Blackwellization.
Anyways, you then end up having to carry around a bunch of
different aggregators in memory, which starts defeating the purpose.

messages.body_plain:
No controversy here, move along (unless you want details).

Specifically, Nishimura and Dunson are simply wrong
in their characterization of "current algorithms" when they
say in the abstract of their arXiv paper:

  The utility of such [HMC] approaches is highlighted in the
  software package STAN ...

  Current algorithms use only the final step, and wastefully
  discard all the intermediate steps.

That's *not* what NUTS does in Stan.  Michael already explained
why the Rao-Blackwellization is more useful for standard HMC
than for NUTS when he commented on the last entry in this thread
that said Radford already showed Rao-Blackwellization helped way
back in 1994 or something like that.

It's sad how badly mischaracterized other people's approaches
are in papers.

- Bob

Apparently I have a bad attitude because I point
out that papers like these are terribly misguided…
Good thing academia is mature and not petty at
all!

In any case, the Nishimura-Dunson paper is
just another scheme for sampling from a trajectory.
In the integration time paper I note that you can
use a slice sampler (as in the original NUTS
implementation) or simple multinomial sampling,
and the Metropolis procedure they do in the paper
would  be a third option.  But it will yield near identical
results for either sampling a single point or doing
a Rao-Blackwellization.

The answer's what I said last time, but let me
elaborate a bit. If you do just the valid cases,
everything works as expected.  When you have NaN
values, they propagate backwards by the chain rule
as

  adjoint += 0 * NaN;

which causes the adjoint to be NaN.

The bigger point is that you need valid argument pairs,
not single sequences of valid arguments.

> Thanks for letting me know. For the binary vectorization code, should we allow the case of scalar-vector/matrix in which the scalar gets promoted to vector/matrix if the nan propagate through? I've thought of a way to test it to avoid this problem, but it would probably avoid testing any combinations that lead to nan derivatives.
>

> Oh, I forgot to mention it's because of the stack order.
> The NaN will wind up lower on the stack and so get propagated
> back even when you're only applying grad() to another variable.
>
> - Bob

> > values, they propagate backwards by the chain rule
> > as
> >
> >   adjoint += 0 * NaN;
> >
> > which causes the adjoint to be NaN.
> >
> > The bigger point is that you need valid argument pairs,
> > not single sequences of valid arguments.

messages.body_plain:
If binary_foo is my binary vectorized function, then these are currently valid function signatures:

binary_foo(stan::math::var x, std::vector<T> y)
binary_foo(std::vector<T> x, stan::math::var y)
binary_foo(stan::math::var x, Eigen::Matrix<stan::math::var, int R, int C> y)
binary_foo(Eigen::Matrix<stan::math::var, int R, int C> x, stan::math::var y)

If x is std::vector<T>, y stan::math::var, fx the return vector, and binary_fun is the function to be vectorized, then the behavior is essentially

for (size_t i = 0; i < x.size(); ++i)
  fx[i] = binary_fun(x[i], y)

Generalizing it to the other signatures, it seems like we might run into this issue with derivatives.

If binary_foo is my binary vectorized function, then these are currently valid function signatures:

binary_foo(stan::math::var x, std::vector<T> y)
binary_foo(std::vector<T> x, stan::math::var y)

messages.body_plain:
That's not general enough.  Each argument should be allowed
to be any of

  var,    vector<var>,    Matrix<var,1,-1>,    Matrix<var,-1,1>,
  double, vector<double>, Matrix<double,1,-1>, Matrix<double,-1,1>,
  int,    vector<int>

So that's 100 instantiations.  It might make sense to do it
with the VectorView template expression.

By "this issue", you mean we still have to figure out how to test
it all?  I think you can just safely segregate the illegal inputs
leading to NaN derivatives and simply not worry about derivatives
anywhere in those cases.

- Bob

> On Apr 29, 2016, at 3:18 PM, Rayleigh L <rayleig...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> If binary_foo is my binary vectorized function, then these are currently valid function signatures:
>
> binary_foo(stan::math::var x, std::vector<T> y)
> binary_foo(std::vector<T> x, stan::math::var y)
> binary_foo(stan::math::var x, Eigen::Matrix<stan::math::var, int R, int C> y)
> binary_foo(Eigen::Matrix<stan::math::var, int R, int C> x, stan::math::var y)
>
> If x is std::vector<T>, y stan::math::var, fx the return vector, and binary_fun is the function to be vectorized, then the behavior is essentially
>
> for (size_t i = 0; i < x.size(); ++i)
>   fx[i] = binary_fun(x[i], y)
>
> Generalizing it to the other signatures, it seems like we might run into this issue with derivatives.
>
> On Fri, Apr 29, 2016 at 3:54 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

messages.body_plain:
Those aren't the only legal signatures; I only gave the ones that I thought were relevant to my question.

My concern is that in live code, it seems that if one derivative is NaN, the whole return vector or matrix will return NaN for its derivative. Is this something to worry about?

On Fri, Apr 29, 2016 at 3:28 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> That's not general enough.  Each argument should be allowed
> to be any of
>
>   var,    vector<var>,    Matrix<var,1,-1>,    Matrix<var,-1,1>,
>   double, vector<double>, Matrix<double,1,-1>, Matrix<double,-1,1>,
>   int,    vector<int>
>
> So that's 100 instantiations.  It might make sense to do it
> with the VectorView template expression.
>
> By "this issue", you mean we still have to figure out how to test
> it all?  I think you can just safely segregate the illegal inputs
> leading to NaN derivatives and simply not worry about derivatives
> anywhere in those cases.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
> > On Apr 29, 2016, at 3:18 PM, Rayleigh L <rayleig...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > If binary_foo is my binary vectorized function, then these are currently valid function signatures:
> >
> > binary_foo(stan::math::var x, std::vector<T> y)
> > binary_foo(std::vector<T> x, stan::math::var y)
> > binary_foo(stan::math::var x, Eigen::Matrix<stan::math::var, int R, int C> y)
> > binary_foo(Eigen::Matrix<stan::math::var, int R, int C> x, stan::math::var y)
> >
> > If x is std::vector<T>, y stan::math::var, fx the return vector, and binary_fun is the function to be vectorized, then the behavior is essentially
> >
> > for (size_t i = 0; i < x.size(); ++i)
> >   fx[i] = binary_fun(x[i], y)
> >
> > Generalizing it to the other signatures, it seems like we might run into this issue with derivatives.
> >
> > On Fri, Apr 29, 2016 at 3:54 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > I couldn't quite parse that.  What's the proposal in terms of
> > signatures and behavior?
> >
> > - Bob

> > > On Apr 28, 2016, at 7:32 PM, Rayleigh L <rayleig...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Thanks for letting me know. For the binary vectorization code, should we allow the case of scalar-vector/matrix in which the scalar gets promoted to vector/matrix if the nan propagate through? I've thought of a way to test it to avoid this problem, but it would probably avoid testing any combinations that lead to nan derivatives.

messages.body_plain:
Not ideal, but no worries for Stan code that's not buggy.

If one of the actual parameter values is NaN or has
a NaN derivative, we're going to reject in all of our
algorithms.

- Bob

> On Apr 29, 2016, at 5:55 PM, Rayleigh L <rayleig...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Those aren't the only legal signatures; I only gave the ones that I thought were relevant to my question.
>
> My concern is that in live code, it seems that if one derivative is NaN, the whole return vector or matrix will return NaN for its derivative. Is this something to worry about?
>
> On Fri, Apr 29, 2016 at 3:28 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> That's not general enough.  Each argument should be allowed
> to be any of
>
>   var,    vector<var>,    Matrix<var,1,-1>,    Matrix<var,-1,1>,
>   double, vector<double>, Matrix<double,1,-1>, Matrix<double,-1,1>,
>   int,    vector<int>
>
> So that's 100 instantiations.  It might make sense to do it
> with the VectorView template expression.
>
> By "this issue", you mean we still have to figure out how to test
> it all?  I think you can just safely segregate the illegal inputs
> leading to NaN derivatives and simply not worry about derivatives
> anywhere in those cases.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
> > On Apr 29, 2016, at 3:18 PM, Rayleigh L <rayleig...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > If binary_foo is my binary vectorized function, then these are currently valid function signatures:
> >
> > binary_foo(stan::math::var x, std::vector<T> y)
> > binary_foo(std::vector<T> x, stan::math::var y)
> > binary_foo(stan::math::var x, Eigen::Matrix<stan::math::var, int R, int C> y)
> > binary_foo(Eigen::Matrix<stan::math::var, int R, int C> x, stan::math::var y)
> >
> > If x is std::vector<T>, y stan::math::var, fx the return vector, and binary_fun is the function to be vectorized, then the behavior is essentially
> >
> > for (size_t i = 0; i < x.size(); ++i)
> >   fx[i] = binary_fun(x[i], y)
> >
> > Generalizing it to the other signatures, it seems like we might run into this issue with derivatives.
> >
> > On Fri, Apr 29, 2016 at 3:54 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > I couldn't quite parse that.  What's the proposal in terms of
> > signatures and behavior?
> >
> > - Bob

> > > On Apr 28, 2016, at 7:32 PM, Rayleigh L <rayleig...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Thanks for letting me know. For the binary vectorization code, should we allow the case of scalar-vector/matrix in which the scalar gets promoted to vector/matrix if the nan propagate through? I've thought of a way to test it to avoid this problem, but it would probably avoid testing any combinations that lead to nan derivatives.
> > >

> > >

messages.body_snippet:
Not ideal, but no worries for Stan code that's not buggy.

If one of the actual parameter values is NaN or has
a NaN derivative, we're going to reject in all of our
algorithms.

- Bob

> On Apr 29, 20

messages.body_plain:
There's an easy way to fix this, which is by refining the adjoint
code to return 0 * NaN as 0, but the test is way to expensive to
insert into every adjoint update, so we leave it this way.

- Bob

> algorithms.
>
> - Bob

insert into every adjoint update, so we leave it this way.
